Sir ROBERT BORDEN laid on the Table, in accordance with an order of the House passed on March 13, 1916, a copy of the pension list in force in Canada for disabled soldiers, and the petitions, letters and other documents relating to the amendment or readjustment of the same.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the said papers were ordered to be printed forthwith, and were referred to a committee composed of Messrs. Green, Hazen, Le-mieux, Macdonald (Pictou), Macdonell (South Toronto), Oliver and Scott, to consider and report upon the rates of pensions so authorized, the establishment of a permanent Pensions Board, and other matters relating thereto or connected therewith.
On the Orders of the Day-:

I am in receipt of a number of letters and telegrams in regard to transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. These letters and telegrams, which are pretty strongly worded, are to the effect that the efforts made to bring the car ferry steamer Prince Edward Island to Charlottetown are not successful; that the steamer is being injured by the strenuous work to which she is subjected in going through the ice; that

the mails are delayed; that travelling is hampered; that trade is tied up, and that apparently a few people in the capital are the cause of the trouble. Charlottetown is the centre of population in Prince Edward Island, and, if the steamer can make trips to that point, that is the place where she ought to call; but if she can not and can make daily trips to Georgetown, it would be wise to have her call there. I would like the minister to consider the matter, because the people are greatly inconvenienced. They allege that the steamer is being injured, and that by some means or other pressure is being brought do bear upon the department to have the steamer call at Charlottetown.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The same instructions have been given to the captain of the car ferry Prince Edward Island that have been given in previous years to the captain of the Minto or whatever boat was maintaining the winter service. Those instructions were to continue the service to Charlottetown so long as it was practicable to do so, having regard' to Weather and ice conditions, and if it was found impossible to maintain that service, then to have the vessel go to Georgetown. Thus the matter is left, as I understand it, in the hands of the captain of the boat. It may be that the steamer now goes less frequently to Georgetown than in previous years; but this, I suppose, is owing to the fact that 'the Prince Edward Island is a stronger icebreaker than the boats formerly engaged in this service. I understand that the Prince Edward Island has missed only one daily trip during the present winter, and that by reason of a heavy snowstorm which prevailed, and it has missed the railway connection only on seventeen days. I will make inquiry into the statement that has reached the- ears of my hon. friend, that the ice conditions being encountered in going to -Charlottetown are so serious that the boat is being somewhat damaged. If that is the case, i-t would be a strong reason why the boat should be diverted from her present route and put upon the Georgetown route.
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, I should be in order to state the information I have received, which does not agree with that received by the minister. I have been informed-
I would call the attention of the hon. member to the rule.
The point I wish to state is not controversial.

If it is the desire of the House that the hon. gentleman should speak, I have no objection; but I would call the attention of the hon. member and of other hon. members to the practice as explained at page 476 of Bourinot:
Questions have been asked, when the orders are called, relative to the state of public business or other matters of public interest: but no discussion should b? allowed when a minister has replied to a question, nor after a member has made his p .rsonal explanation.
Of course if no objection' is taken to the hon. member speaking, I shall raise none.
It is a personal explanation.

I would rather give it now, if I am permitted.
Order.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will send me a memorandum stating the information he has, I will have the matter looked into at once.
On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to call the attention of the acting Minister of Railways to the car situation on the Intercolonial railway. Yesterday I received from a large firm dealing in lumber and pulpwood in Quebec City a letter, from which I will Tead two or three lines:
We thought we would drop you a line in regard to the car situation on the Intercolonial railway. For the past two months we have been supplied with very few cars for our pulp-wood shipments to the States and when we have received cars, in some eases they have remained on the sidings where loaded for several weeks waiting to be moved.
The Intercolonial railway officials give as their excuse that the weather conditions were very unfavourable and that they are very short of power to move both empties and loaded cars, and in consequence it is impossible for them to do anything.
Can my hon. friend give me some information with regard to the car shortage and can he alleviate it in any way? Because I understand from this letter that the situation is very serious and that the lumbermen especially are very much hampered in their shipments on this account.

I am aware that there has been a little trouble on the Intercolonial, but not more, perhaps not as much as on the
other railways throughout the Dominion. The hon. member knows that during the last month or six weeks, not only the Intercolonial, but almost every other railway in Canada has been tied up by the great snow storms. The Intercolonial as done good iwork ini pushing traffic through as well as it has done in spite of the snow blockade. The motive power has been used largely to get the passenger trains through, and tlhe trains conveying troops. In addition to that, munitions and war supplies have been given the right of way. It is absolutely necessary to get that freight *through to load the transports waiting at Halifax and St. John. For these reasons, local freight has had to be delayed a little more than would have been the case otherwise. In Montreal the yards, not only of the Intercolonial but of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific, [DOT] have been filled to their utmost capacity with cars held up by the blockade. I received a telegram yesterday from the general manager of the Intercolonial, and have asked for one to-day, dealing with the situation. In yesterday's message it was stated that the Intercolonial was clear, was running 175 cars a day, and anticipated no more trouble. I feel sure that the trouble with regard to local freight will soon be overcome. The people along the line must have a little patience on account of the absolute necessity of moving war supplies.
I think the hon. gentleman will agree that war supplies and munitions must take precedence.	.
On'the Orders of the Day:

As a matter of importance, I would like to draw the attention of the Acting Minister of Railways to a letter I have received from my home town, Chatham, N.B., to the effect that the station-master there has instructions not to receive freight for local points. One of the important shippers there required to send supplies to Blackville, a tpwn twenty-five miles away on a branch line, but the station-master refuseci the freight. The grievance that this letter expresses is that freight is 'being received at Newcastle station billed to the same point, Blackville. The shipper claims that he is at a disadvantage. I would ask the minister if he would give instructions that the town of Chatham be treated in this regard as liberally as other towns.
I will have the matter looked into. The same reply that I gave to the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) applies to this.
Chatham is on a branch line.	*
We will try to have it put on the main line, so far as freight is concerned.
On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to call the attention of the Government, or whomever is responsible, to the use made of the reading room by members. It is quite a common practice for members to take away newspapers and keep them in their rooms. Those in charge of the reading room have no means of knowing who have possession of any newspapers so taken. If the reading room is for the benefit of a few members, I suppose this method is all right, but if it is for the benefit of the members generally, the newspapers ought to be there at all reasonable hours, at any rate. I believe that those who want newspapers in their rooms should subscribe for them. I merely call attention to this matter, as the evil seems to be growing. It has become worse since we moved to this building, notwithstanding that the facilities for reading in this reading room are better than in the old building.
Orders will be given to the curator which will put a stop to the practice complained of.

I find that a number of
the newspapers in the reading room have important articles clipped from them. That is something that does not reflect credit upon the members of the House who are guilty of it.

Qn motion of Sir George Foster, Bill No. 58, to amend the Canada Grain Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section-1 poiver of Board to order supply of cars:

I explained the purpose of this Bill to the House the other day, and asked the members from the northwest who were particularly interested in it *to consider it in order that, if possible, it

might be passed with expedition when next taken up. It is a matter of moment; quick action upon it is necessary. Those members who heard my explanation the other day will understand the purport of the Bill. In a few words, its purpose is this: a large amount of grain in the West, particularly in some of the most congested districts, has not the benefit of warehousing or of elevator storage; it is simply lying in the fields. A great deal of this grain is in bins without floors. As long as the weather continues bright and cold, even if snowy, the grain will suffer practically no injury, but as soon as a thaw takes place the snow which is upon the grain will melt, and the grain will be liable to speedy damage. Car-order arrangements are matters of enactment. In section 207 of the Grain Act, after what you may call the standard arrangements for carordering are set forth, certain discretion is given to the Board of Railway Commissioners. That discretion is contained in four lines. The present Act says:
The board may in its discretion order cars to be supplied contrary to the provisions of this part, (a) to elevators that are in danger of collapse: Ob) to places where grain is damp and thereby liable to become damaged, (c) for the purpose of distributing seed grain to any point in the western division, and (d) in cases where the operator of any country elevator reports in writing under oath that some portion of the grain in such elevator is heated, and that in order to preserve such grain it is necessary to ship such heated grain to a terminal elevator for treatment.
The provision (b) allows discretion to the board in cases where grain is damp. The purpose of this amendment is to give the Board of Grain Commissioners disc; etiou to order cars for the carrying of this grain" in cases where it is liable to damage.
Will that work in harmony writh the amendment to the Railway Act which was passed the other day?

Yes, except that the Railway Act refers to large sections, and to the operation of different lines of railway as to carrying points. This eues into detail, while the other was a matter of more general application. I may say that this amendment has been very strongly urged upon the Commissioners and upon the department by the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan. I have a long letter from him to the commissioners in which he makes a very strong plea for the immediate enactment of such legislation.

I imagine that anything that I can say will not affect the decision of the minister in regard to this provision.

My view is that every purpose that is ostensibly to be served by this amendment is already covered by subsection "b". The grain lying uncovered in the fields is in danger of destruction only from dampness, and if the point is taken that at the moment it is not damp, and, therefore, does not come under subsection "b", my view would certainly be that we should adhere to the principle of the (Bill and provide specifically for that particular case, rather than, by a provision such as this, simply destroy that feature of the Grain Act which has been most strongly held to 'by the farmers of the West, in season and out of season and und.er all circumstances. The principle of compelling the distribution of cars according to priority of order has been fought by every interest opposed to the farmer in the West. I am compelled to say that my hon. friend has to some degree already listened to these opposing interests, and in this section he proposes absolutely to place the grain at their disposal so far as the principle of the car-ord,er book is concerned. If this section passes, in my humble judgment, we can consider that that feature of the Grain Act is eliminated, and. that the right that the farmers have stood for during so many years, the right for which they have fought so hard, and which they have maintained so strongly, is taken away from them without good or sufficient reason.
At whose suggestion did the hon. minister say that this legislation is introduced?
The Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan, Mr. Motherwell.
Is there correspondence about it?	'
Yes.
Could we see it?

I can read a portion of it, if that would satisfy my hon. friend.
Sir WILFRID LAURlER: Hear, hear.

The correspondence began with a request by Mr. Motherwell that discretionary power should be given to the Board of Grain, Commissioners in order to meet this very pressing difficulty during the present season. The board replied to the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan that whilst they were entirely in sympathy with the purpose that he had
in view, they were devoid of power, because they could use their discretion only in certain specific instances. They pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan that the very discretion which he wished to be granted to the Grain Commissioners in ord,er to alleviate tnis trouble had been applied for when the Act was being amended some two or three years ago. That provision had been passed by the House of Commons, but had been thrown out by the Senate. This reply was sent to Mr. Motherwell, who, after looking up the facts of the case, wrote to the effect, that he found that the Board of Commissioners was entirely right in that matter. He urged then that that discretionary power be applied for.
Mr. Motherwell, in a letter to Dr. Magill, Chief Commissioner, says:
It would take Parliament possibly an hour to pass this subsection through its various stages, including the Royal Assent, and I am strongiy of the opinion that it should he done. We cannot afford to fiddle over this business much longer as spring is rapidly approaching. It has been thawing here all week and in western Saskatchewan the Chinook has caused the streets of towns like Swift Current to run' with water,. A few more days like this, and the damage to the grain in question will begin. Surely, we are not to stand helplessly by indulging in further speculation as to what should he done and wait until the wheat actually is damaged so that it can he shipped out under subsection " b " of section 207 of the Canada Grain Act.
The Grain Commissioners do not believe that they have the power to act until the grain is actually proved to be damp. It may be that it is not damp under present conditions, but if it is left until it becomes damp, so that the Board of Grain Commissioners have power to act, the damage will have been done and it will be too late to salve the grain. Very gratifying reports come from the vicinities- of Saskatoon, Moosejaw and Calgary with reference to the usefulness of the Government storage elevators in these different sections. Quantities of damaged and damp grain have been brought in. We have the finest cleaning and drying arrangements that are possible in connection with these elevators, and thousands of bushels have already been salved and cleaned. A despatch this morning from the elevator at Saskatoon says that pretty nearly 3,000,000 bushels have been passed through that elevator and some 2,000,000 bushels are now in storage. That is a point at which the railway arrangements particularly effect the quick passage of grain. The Canadian Northern

railway is bringing out grain on short hauls from the congested districts and storing it in Saskatoon. The Grand Trunk is carrying it to the East; so that the transfer through the elevator is continuously going on; farmers get their certificates and their weights and are able to make their financial arrangements. They also have the advantage of having clean grain if they wish it, and they have it dried if it becomes damp. If subsection " b " covered the case, we would not want to ask for extra legislation. But in the opinion of the board and of the Minister of Agri-_ culture of Saskatchewan, it does not cover the case,

The trouble is that the amendment is addressing itself to the solution of a problem that perhaps should not be solved. The minister says that wherever there is congestion they can order this to be done. It is not congestion that is going to be the reason or justification for favouring any particular point. The congestion might be ever so great, but the principle that car orders should be given to people equitably should still prevail, and the congestion be left to be relieved in the ordinary course of events. If the minister provided that this board should have the exceptional power, not because there is congestion, but because the grain is damp or in real danger of becoming damp, he would be addressing himself to the state of circumstances that the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan seems to dwell upon. The subclause under section 207 of the Grain Act which is involved is:
The hoard may, in its discretion, order cars to he provided contrary to the provisions of this part.... (b) to places where grain is damp and thereby liable to become damaged.
Why should not the minister, in the wording of his amendment, continue to confine himself to the kind of grain that is to be handled, and not open up the whole thing and give the board discretion to favour certain places because there is what, in the board's opinion, constitutes congestion?
, Would it not be better for the minister to have his amendment read:	"To places
where grain has become or is in real danger of becoming damp." Or better words which the minister would find on reflection Why break in on the principle of equitable car distribution simply on account of con-jestion?

If there were
no congestion there would be no necessity

for this clause. These men have grain lying in the fields, sometimes eighteen or twenty thousand bushels, without any covering, and liable to these processes as soon as the weather becomes mild and the snow begins to melt. If there were no congestion there would be no call for this, because there would be plenty of cars and the grain could be carried away. The trouble is that there is congestion and that car orders are in in advance of the orders of the man who has grain which is in a perilous position, and, unless there is something to step in between the general rule and that pile of grain, that grain is almost certain to be seriously injured. I think that where a man has grain stored under such conditions that it is not likely to be injured, his car orders ought to wait until the man alongside of him who has grain stored without the advantage of cover of any kind has had his grain moved.

There may be and has been congestion at many shipping points where the wheat is not in any danger. If the minister reads Mr. Motherwell's correspondence, he will see that Mr. Motherwell treats it largely as a geographical matter, referring to the fact that in the older districts, such as eastern Saskatchewan and all of Manitoba, although very often there is congestion there, yet the people are provided with facilities for storing grain on their farms; and so, although there might be congestion, there would be no peril or danger of the grain being lost, whereas in the newer places farther west the homesteaders, under more pioneer conditions, might he exposed to much greater danger of loss, even although the congestion were less. I do not think the minister should put upon us the grave responsibility of defeating this legislation, or of refusing it. We explained to him that all we, ask is that the Board of Grain Commissioners attend to the condition of affairs it is sought to relieve. We have congestion all through the winter at some of those points, but the danger does not come until the spring. The board might exercise that discretion at points where there was no danger of any dampness damaging the wheat, and relieve the situation at other points, as they are empowered to do. I do not think that the minister should place us on the horns of a dilemma in that way. All we ask is that this amendment be again amended to meet the condition of affairs. Many farmers would not object to letting the congestion remain, or to letting the wheat lie for a while until their brother

farmers in the pioneer districts had got relief, because the danger of damage to the grain is a great deal more pronounced there than in the older districts where they have granaries. I think my hon. friend the minister will see that our quarrel is not with the principle but with the wording of his amendment. '

My plea would
be this: Provide for the known and uniform cases by actual enactment, and then leave this matter in	charge of the
Board of Grain Commissioners.	They
know the circumstances better than any of us can here, and if it is wise to give them discretion to go beyond those points, I do not think the House will make any mistake in just leaving the matter to their discretion. The point of urgency for the legislation comes just from the circumstances that my hon. friend has mentkmed, that in those districts at which we are looking at the present time there is a congestion of grain which is not housed. It is not a question of a man having his grain where it would not be damaged, and being able to wait for his cars. He is not being injured so far as the quality of his grain is concerned, but it is a case where a very large quantity of this grain is piled up on the open prairie, and if it remains there a month longer1 it will probably be very much damaged, if not absolutely spoiled. Whilst we are at it, we might just as well have some faith in human nature, and trust to the Grain Commission to do what is fair in the matter, as try to tie them down to every small detail of what may occur to us here in the Houser I do not think my hon. friend will be injured by that stretch of magnanimity.

The minister has asked
the House and the country to trust the Grain Commission. The whole purpose of the Grain Act is to depend on legislative enactment, rather than on official discretion. If his point is right, there is no reason why the Grain Act should remain on the -statute book. Now that we have a Grain -Commission, which is supposed to know more about the grain business than anybody else, we might just a-s- well, if we are to follow his argument, trust them in -everything, and say: The matter of the -control and handling of the western grain is in your hands; do with it as you please, and for the bes-t, and wipe the Grain Act off the statute. That is the logic of the minister's argument, I do not think that he will be prepared
to-day to carry his argument to its logical conclusion. I do not think he will be prepared to ask this House to wipe the Grain Act off the statute-book, and yet if there is any provision in the Grain Act that the farmers lay store by, and lay stress on, that they demand shall be kept away from anybody's discretion as far as possible, it is this provision in regard to car distribution. Wipe that ou-t and you might just as well wipe the Grain Act off the statute book; there is no protection in it so far as the farmer is concerned. I maintain that the provisions of subsection " b " as they stand cover the case that has been presented to the House by the min-siter. I take issue with the Grain Commission if they hold a contrary view, and I call upon the minister to interpret for them the proper meaning of the Act and their duties, and to see that they carry them out. My hon. friend the minister has said that the grain is going to be dampened when the warm weather comes if it remains piled up on the prairie. Has he not read the papers? Does he not know that warm weather has been experienced there for the past four or five weeks, that in the town of Walsh in the dry belt of the Canadian Pacific railway the people have been flooded out. Southern Alberta has been subject to a Chinook. The snow has gone and the grain is damp. It must always be .so. Thousands -a-nd -tens of thousands of bushels of damp g-r-ain have been taken into the elevators. The -condition of dampness is already great, actual dampness and damage, and therefore subsection "b" is in full effect, -so far as the grain of Southern Alberta and Southern Saskatchewan js concerned. I say again that if, when grain is piled on the prairie and covered with -snow, the Grain Commission, with the purpose and intent of subsection "b" staring them in the face, deny that that grain comes under the discretion granted by that subsection, that Grain Commission, I will say here on my responsibility as a member of this House, is not honest in the discharge of its duties, and requires to be disciplined by the minister in the interest of that industry which he and they -are in their positions to protect.
Does the minister not think himself that that clause covers it?

I do not, and 1 would not take the responsibility of -saying that the Grain Commission should remove the grain which is now piled on the open

prairie, where the weather has not turned soft, even if it may he covered with snow. I would not ask them to read into their instructions under that subsection the power to remove that grain if it is not damaged. They have evidently had the subject under consideration, and they do not think they have such powers, and they have not exercised those powers. I am not going to instruct them to do so. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says if they have not that discretion, we might as well repeal the whole Act. We have given them discretion in four points already. There is no business man in the world, no corporation, no legislator in the world, no business anywhere which does more than provide for general policy, and general principles, leaving in t'he hands of the management certain discretionary powers. You have to do it; you cannot get along in business without doing it. Something turns up that no 'legislator thought of, that no director had provided for, and you have to have a certain amount of discretionary power. In regard to the Grain Commission, the House acknowledge that, and gave them discretionary powers. *It is now asked that these discretionary powers be extended so as to cover these cases. That is all we ask, and I did not suppose that the House would offer any objection.

I am sorry that - the minister feels so surprised. The last time I referred to the subject-I do not think the minister was present-the Minister of Railways said that he would have a statement made up to date as to how much grain they had taJken into the Government elevators.
And I understand that there is what we call an embargo until the fifteenth of this month. As it affects the question of this hauling of grain, it is more particularly under the Railway Department. But the embargo has the effect, as I understand it, that priority is given to cars that are used only for the purpose of hauling grain to the elevator as against the cars which may be tied up for two or three weeks going all the way to Fort William. That is something that concerns the grain trade very much although I rather question if it is not technically a matter which the Railway Commission, under Sir Henry Drayton, has under its jurisdiction. I understand that it has worked out very well and that, whereas when I referred to the matter in the House late in January or early in Feb-

ruary, there was a very small percentage of the capacity of the internal elevators filled. I understand that since a very much greater quantity of grain has gone into the elevators. If my information is right, that it is proposed to take that embargo off at the middle of this month, I would ask the minister whether it would not be well to continue it until these elevators are filled right up.
I think I might suggest to my hon. friend that this is a matter which does not directly affect the passage of this amendment.
I think it has a great deal to do with it
Perhaps my hon. friend thinks so. If he does it is a matter for himself.
It relieves the same situation that this relieves.

It does relieve it, because it ehables more grain to be carried out than otherwise would be. Do what you can, you get by the short hauls a large amount of this grain hauled out at this period of the year, or about the first of March, but you still leave a very large quantity of grain which will not have been moved even when March, or April, is done. The usual effect of the short haul business has been to increase the efficiency of the service by the railways. Instead of making the trains carry the grain from distant districts all the way through to Fort William, or to eastern elevators, it is carried by means of the short haul to the central elevator and then the cars go back and get other loads. They probably make half a dozen hauls where they would only make one haul to the eastern, or lake head, elevator. That is working very satisfactorily. I cannot give my hon. friend the exact number of bushels that have gone to each elevator, but all the elevators are filling up and the Saskatoon and Moosejaw elevators are emptying out as well as filling up and thus the grain is kept moving. But the point now is as to this particular amendment. I do not want to press the committee at all but Iamobligedto go away a little past four o'clock and I
4 p.m. would 'like that we should confine our remarks as nearly as possible to.the amendment in hand so that if possible I may get the Bill through before I have to go away.

The minister runs a good department and he keeps the grain administration very tree from politics and I shall not say anything unfavourable ' to him. If there is one part of the Administration that is run in a very high class way, it is the minister's conduct of the grain business and I do not want to cross, him at all. But the question of the equitable distribution of cars is the lock, *stock and barrel of the Grain Act. While the minister does not see it as I do, I am sorry that I feel it to be my duty to place myself on record as to the amendment that the minister introduces and I therefore propose that the following be adopted:
That we amend clause " b " of section 207 of the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27, hy adding, after the word " damp " in line 4, the words " or unhoused."
It would then give the Board power to order cars to places where the grain is damp, or unhoused, and thereby liable to become damaged.

This matter has been brought to my attention by the Board, which has given it very careful consideration. The Board has asked for the powers of discretion which I have provided for in the amendment, and I would rather stand behind the Board and give them that discretion and thus restrict the matter by two details, or one detail, in addition to what is given in subsection "b" than to provide other means for discretion being used by the Board under equally pressing circumstances and with results which would equally imperil in some degree the grain left uncarried. I would like to ask the committee to pass the legislation which has been asked for by the Board and which I have submitted to it.

I trust the minister will still make up his mind to accept the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), or something to that effect. I feel very much as other western friends do, that I do not want to throw anything in the way of the minister in this matter. But I have to ask the minister to remember that he is getting back to the old fight that we have been carrying on for the last twenty years or more, and the western farmers feel that a great deal is at stake in connection with the passing of such an amendment as this. We have fought our fight, a very bitter one, not only against the elevators, but also against the railway companies and other institutions of that kind. The-railway companies
in the early days insisted that all grain must be shipped through elevators. We had a hard time, as my hon. friend knows, to get the right to ship out cars on order. This question has been up in the House before, and some discussion has taken place. The farmers of the West realize that if you pass such an amendment as this it will mean that the commission, or some other body, will have the power to say that the regular order shall be deviated from when there is grain damaged or in danger of being damaged, or when the elevators want more cars than they are entitled to according to the strict provisions of the Act. I know very well that the feeling that the farmers of the West will have in regard to this matter is that it is simply a way of getting back to the old elevator monopoly. I share very largely that suspicion with the farmer, and I would be very glad indeed if the minister could see his way to accept the amendment of my hon. friend from Moosejaw, or something of the like effect, and not get us up against this important question that we have been up against so often. It is a very serious question, and one that we should not be put' up against any more.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It does not appear to me that the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) is an amendment to the Bill under consideration. As I understand it, the Bill is for the purpose of adding subsection " e " to section 207 of the Grain Act. The proposed amendment of the hon. member for Moosejaw is to amend subsection "b" of the Grain Act, so that it is not, in my judgment, an amendment to the proposed amendment. In other words, the proposed Bill could he passed and it would still be open to the hon. member to move a further amendment; but his motion is in no way an amendment to the Bill before the committee. .
Mr.'PUGSLEY:	1 understand that my
hon. friend suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this amendment be substituted for the one now before the committee. In order to put it in proper form, all that would be necessary would be to say that section so-and-so be struck out and so-and-so be substituted therefor. I assume that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not take any advantage of the point, because it is so easy to correct it.

I have no intention of taking any advantage. What I want is to have the best legislation possible; but

I have a conviction that the proposed amendment of my hon. friend is not the best legislation, and that this House would be wise to stand by the recommendation of the Board of Grain Commissioners, backed up as it is by the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan. My hon. friend (Mr. Thomson) referred to the old fight; but we are no longer back on the ground of that old fight. The conditions were very different then, as my hon. friend knows, and he would have to imagine that the Grain Board would join hands with the railway companies and the elevator men to get the position of the last few years reversed. I assure him that is not the wish of the department, nor is it the wish of the Board of Grain Commissioners. I still think my hon. friend will sleep well at night even if this section is appended to the Bill.

So far as Manitoba, and even so far as that part of Saskatchewan which my hon. friend represents, is concerned, this makes very little difference; but farther West there is no doubt that it does make a difference. If my information is correct, the Board of Grain Commissioners are already using, but in an illegal way, the discretion which they are asking for in this proposed amendment. I understand that from conversations with the Grain Commissioners.

In my judgment, the
amendment of the hon. member for Moose-jaw covers exactly the point that the hon. minister wishes to cover, that is, to look after grain that is liable to be damaged. I think it is a very praiseworthy and necessary action to take; but if the amendment of the hon. member for Moosejaw covers the point sufficiently, why amend the Act-in the way proposed by the minister!-' While I have every confidence that the Board of Grain Commissioners would carry out the proposed amendment properly and fairly, and use it only with regard to grain likely to be damaged, at the same time there is a great deal in what my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) has said. The farmers are very jealous over the privilege of equal distribution of cars, and there has been -all along a desire and an attempt on the part of the railways to get aw,ay from it; and if you have the railways and the Grain Commissioners working together, with the law giving them power to send cars where-ever they wish, you will put the farmers in the position that they will never be sure of getting cars when they want them, and

even if they -are getting fair play in many cases, they will feel, when they do not get the cars they want, that it is owing to this amendment now proposed by the minister. There would be nothing more objectionable to the farmers than to have , to go back to the old position where the railways and the Board of Grain Commissioners would have the say as to the distribution of cars. .
Mr. Chairman, since you ruled my amendment out of order I have been trying to put it in order-or is that point waived?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not at all.

My hon. friend will have to put himself in order and move an amendment which is germane to the Bill. He has a perfect right to do that. Mr. KNOWLES: Bill 58 says:
Section 207 of the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27 of the statutes of 1912 is amended-
It is section 207 that we are proceeding by legislation to amend. The minister proceeds to amend it in one way and I proceed to amend it in another, -and, with all deference to you, Mr. Chairman, it seems - to me that my amendment was in order, because it was an amendment to section 207 by way of substitution,.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment as proposed by the hon. member is an amendment to section 207 of the Canada Grain Act, but it is something entirely foreign to that portion of the section which is proposed to be amended by this Bill. My hon. friend, in his amendment, which I ruled out of order, proposed:
That we amend clause " b " of section 207 of the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27, by adding after the word " damp " in line four, the words " or unhoused."
This Bill does not propose to amend subsection "b" of section 207 at all; it proposes to add a further subsection to the existing section.
I take the view that we are not amending any particular subsection, but that we are amending section 207. I will put it in this way.

Will my hon. friend allow .me to make a suggestion in order to facilitate matters and ease the conscience of hon. gentlemen opposite? Suppose we amend the section in this way:
Whenever after due examination the board considers necessary and advisable, in order to relieve congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain which is insufficiently housed and liable to become damp-	.

I am willing to make that amendment, *and I think that is as far as I can possibly ge.

Would not the minister just transpose certain words and. say:
Whenever after due examination the board considers it necessary and advisable, in order to facilitate the despatch of grain which is insufficiently housed and liable to become damp, and to relieve congestion in respect thereto-

I read it in this way. It is advisable in order to relieve congestion-in wh'at respect? In the facilitation of the despatch of grain which is insufficiently housed or liable to become damp or injured.
In the way my hon. friend has it, the commissioners will be likely to read "or" in place of "and." By transposing the words you would, make the amendment clear to every one.
, That the following words be added after the word " grain " : " that is insufficiently housed and liable to become damp or injured."

That may limit it to
grain not housed and liable to be injured; but it seems to me to divide the provision into two, which would give the commission authority to send cars where there is congestion and the grain is not liable to injury' Mr. KNOWLES: I do not wish to impose on the minister, but I am going to try him with this:
Whenever after due examination the board considers it necessary and advisable, in order to relieve congestion in respect of grain which remains unhoused and is by reason thereof liable to suffer damage
I am afraid that is so involved that the Grain Commissioners would not understand it.

Would the minister say
that in his judgment the amendment he proposes does confine the discretion of the Grain Commission to grain that is unhoused?

I find it easier to legislate, or rather to propose- legislation, than to give a judgment as to how the legislation will be interpreted. But I think that is very largely the way I would interpret it. If there is any extra discretion, that is provided for. I do not think it would militate against the operation of the Act.

It would seem to me
that the Minister of Trade and Commerce 108
wishes to meet the views of the members from the West, but he is afraid to interfere with the phraseology of the Bill as sent to him by the Grain Commission.

You can put
it that way if you like.
How does the hon. gentleman want to put it?
Any way that will suit you.
No, I will put it to suit the hon. gentleman. He says he does not undertake to interpret the law. I think he did study law once.
I found out what it was like and left it.

Like the student who was in the lawyer's office for two days and left saying he had learned enough to disgust him with the whole business. In this section the minister has the words: " To relieve -congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain which remains unhoused." If he does not know, the very excellent lawyer who occupies the position of Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain), than whom there is no better lawyer in Canada-
1( stuck to it.

-and wisely, too; the
Postmaster General will tell the hon. gentleman that icnuris very often interpret "and" as "or," and vice versa. And the Grain Commission, which may be called a court, may interpret this "in order to relieve congestion ' or ' facilitate the despatch of grain." Now, the hon. gentleman does not mean that. Why use the word "congestion" by itself? Why not say, "congestion in respect of grain -that remains unhoused and is thereby li-able to suffer damage?" That is so plain that it could hardly be misunderstood.
Does not the commission wish to go further?
No.
I understand they do.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks not. If he leaves this as it is, the -commission will say: "Some stupid person has put "and" there when he means "or." It does not mean anything unless it was intended to give the commission discretion with Tespect to other grain than that which remains unhoused. The minister has said he intends it to apply



to unhoused grain which by reason thereof is liable to damage. If he does mean that, why does he not say that in express words, so that there will be no doubt as to the meaning?

I think my hon. friend went a little further than my words would justify. I did assume that there might be a modicum or discretion which might be directed towards points which were congested, even if the element of damp or injured grain was not involved, ind I wish that to form a part of the amendment itself. Now, we have pretty well discussed this matter; let us express our minds about it and go on with further business; otherwise, I shall be obliged to ask the committee to rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again; and probably the point between us is not sufficient to make that necessary.

I will place my amendment on record. I move:
That all the words after the word "amended" in the second line he struck out and the following: substituted : " By Inserting the words ' or unhoused ' after the word ' damp ' in the fourth line of said section 207."
I move that specially because the minister has said that the purpose is to give the Grain Commissioners discretionary power to relieve congestion where there is no danger of the grain suffering, and, foi my part, I am absolutely against that. If I understand the minister's purpose, then there is a great difference between the way he looks at it and the way I look at it. _

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have only this moment seen this proposed amendment, but, as I understand it, it is not an amendment to the amendment that is already before the committee. I would submit, Mr. Chairman that this proposed legislation is to amend section 207 of the Grain Act, " by adding thereto."

Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for a committee to inquire into purchases of shells or other munitions or goods by the Shell Committee, resumed from Thursday, March 9.

My right hon. friend the Prime
Minister, toward the close of his speech on this resolution, made a very important statement, which will be found in Hansard, on page 1592. Referring to the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who moved this resolution, the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
If, however, he or any of his followers has a charge to make against any member of the Government with respect to the Shell Committee or with respect to anything else, let him or his follower stand up in his place, and on his responsibility as a member, make that charge, and it will be investigated thoroughly and completely.
Later on he says:
But there is something else to be said, and I repeat that if my right hon. friend or any of his followers has any charge to make against a member of the Government in regard to any of these matters, let him make that charge in distinct and understandable terms, and he will have the investigation as soon as he so desires.
The hon. member for Carleton, N.B., in supporting the resolution, presented to this House an array of facts in reference to purchases which were made by this Shell Committee of, I think you will agree with me, Sir, a most startling character; facts given with circumstantiality and detail, which must have convinced hon. members of this House, as I know7 they convinced the country, that the hon. member for Carleton had definite and positive information of the matters of which he was speaking. In view of the statements made by my right- hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in moving the resolution; and in view ori all the information which has

been given to the House, I should have supposed that the charges made were sufficiently definite and of a sufficiently grave character not only to justify but to demand an immediate investigation by a committee of this House. But, Sir, my right hon. friend has stated that he desires that some member of the House shall put these charges in direct and understandable form. I suppose he means that they should be put in concrete form; that some member of this House should rise in his place and take upon himself personally the responsibility of making a charge against the Government or some member of the Government in respect to the matters with which the Shell Committee has dealt. The reason for that is, as you know, to prevent the time of Parliament being taken up with the investigation of charges with regard to which a member of the House is not prepared to take responsibility as such member. You know, Sir, as well as I, what are the consequences which fall upon a member of the House if he is found to have made charges of a character which cannot be substantiated. He will not only be treated with contempt in the House, but the consequence which falls upon him ordinarily and almost necessarily is that he is obliged to forfeit his seat. Well, Sir, speaking as a member of this House, and realizing as I do the gravity of the charges which are made against the Shell Committee as the appointees of this Government, and also necessarily against the Minister of Militia as a member of this Government who made the appointments of that committee and was constantly in touch, as he says, with that committee, and to whom that committee reported from week to week, as we have had it in evidence; I, Sir, knowing the facts and knowing how grave they are; knowing how grave was the charge which, as I have said, was made against the Shell Committee and the Minister of Militia; knowing what vast sums are involved; knowing, Sir, that the evidence has disclosed to this House that in connection with the $300,000,000 and upwards of contracts given by the Shell Committee there has been, beyond the shadow of a doubt, absolutely wasted upwards of $80,000,000-somewhere between $80,000,000 and $100,000,000 of the money of the people of Great Britain and the people of Canada-Sir, I feel that I would be derelict in my duty, I would be acting the part of a coward and of one unworthy to occupy the position of a representative of an important constituency of this Do-1084
minion, if I were to hesitate to take upon myself the responsibility of'accepting the invitation which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has given, and of putting these charges in concrete and understandable form, and bringing upon myself the responsibility which will devolve upon me and which will properly devolve upon me-if I should, in case a committee is granted, fail to make good the charges which have been presented to this House. I accept the responsibility; and now, Sir, (reading):
I, William Pugsley, a member of this House, in support of the motion now under consideration, standing in my place in this House and on my responsibility as a member of this House, declare and charge that the Shell Committee, appointed by the Minister of Militia and referred to in said motion, fixed excessive and unreasonable prices for shells and for other munitions and goods to be furnished to the British Government (which by arrangement between the British Government and the Canadian Government were to be paid for in part by Canada.)
That such prices were fixed without competition and were far in excess of what would necessarily have been paid if ordinary business methods had been pursued, thereby involving an unnecessary excessive expenditure of many millions of dollars, conservatively estimated at at least eighty millions, which will be improperly taken from the people of the United Kingdom and Canada.
That said committee gave large orders at such excessive prices and without competition to companies in which members of the committee weTe largely interested, and of some of which companies members of the said committee were the directing heads.
That there has been great and wholly unnecessary delay in furnishing the completed shells for use of the Canadian and British forces at the front.
That the said Shell Committee neglected and delayed for an undue period of time to provide the fuses necessary to render the shells effective, and, failing to endeavour to provide for their construction in Canada, as they might have done, proceeded to give and award, through J. Wesley Allison in the United States, contracts for fuses amounting to $22,000,000, on which they made an advance of $3,750,000. That the making of the said contracts through said Allison was unwise and improvident and was entered into with the knowledge

and connivance of the Minister of Militia, and the said Shell Committee failed to Obtain, delivery of said fuses for an unreasonable time.
And I do also charge that the Government of Canada had, through the Minister of Militia, to whom the said Shell Committee reported weekly, knowledge of such irregular -and improper methods and acts of the said Shell Committee, and while having the power at any time to put an end thereto the said minister improperly consented to such irregular and improper methods and acts and permitted the same to continue.
Having read this charge, I submit it for the consideration of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and the consideration of the members of,this House. I shall deal with it a little later on, and for the moment I shall devote attention to some remarks which were made by^the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. E. B. Bennett). I am bound to say, Sir, that I do not find much to answer in the speech of that hon. gentleman. His speech was a very eloquent one; it was a very interesting one. That speech stamps the hon. gentleman as one of the most forceful and able and eloquent members" on the other side of the House. That gentleman has had many opportunities of getting inside knowledge of what has been going on in connection with the purchase of munitions for the Canadian and British Governments. Ever since that most valuable and honoured member of this House broke away from this Government on an important occasion when this Parliament was asked to- ratify an agreement made with one of the important railroads of this country, and which that hon. gentleman denounced in the strongest possible terms, this Government, Sir, have shown a very conciliatory course towards the hon. member for Calgary. They are determined that he shall not get away from them again. If I am correctly informed, the Prime Minister scarcely ever takes a trip abroad without inviting the hon. member to accompany him. He even accompanied the Prime Minister as far as the trenches, and I saw by the papers that he had gone ,as the personal attendant and personal adviser of my right Ihon. friend the Prime Minister. Well, Sir, that hon. gentleman has not ventured to challenge the accuracy of the figures which were presented to this House by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). Need I argue that it was because it could not be done? The hon. member for Calgary is industrious and is

most able and most intelligent, and if it had been possible to question the accuracy of the figures or statements presented by that hon. member, you may depend, and I am sure this House will agree with me, that the hon. member for Calgary would have devoted himself to that task. He did not do so. He did not discuss whether or not excessive prices had been paid. He said he had nothing in the world to do with the question whether or	not "orders for
shells had been given to members of the Shell Committee or to companies in which they were interested, or to cousins or uncles or aunts or other relatives of themselves. That was a matter of no interest to him. All that he was concerned about was that while the war is on we should not investigate these matters, no matter how horrible they might be, and no matter how much might be shown against the Shell Committee. He compared the position of those of us who wanted an investigation to that of a man whose house was burning and who wanted the firemen to cease their operations while he began to examine into the cost of the hose that was being used for the purpose of extinguishing the fire. My hon. friend went further and said that the boots ought never to have been inquired into by this House, and he rather found fault with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister for granting the boots inquiry. He said he had been pressed unduly from some quarter, what quarter he did not say, to have the investigation; but he ventured to say that the Prime Minister would not repeat the experiment and have an inquiry into matters concerning the Shell Committee.	*
What was the argument used by my hon. friend? Why, he said, the result of that investigation was to prevent Canadian boot manufacturers from getting very large orders in France, because the people of that country had become convinced that Canadian boots were not as they ought to be. With those patriotic gentlemen on the *other side of the House it is all a question of money, apparently. It did 'not seem to impress the hon. gentlemen's mind that there was complaint with regard to the boots which were furnished to the Canadian soldiers-that letters were coming from the front stating that the bools were unfit to wear. My hon. friend was not impressed with the fact that the newspapers of Canada were clamouring for an investigation before that inquiry took place, claiming that a great injustice was being

clone to the .soldiers by providing them with defective boots. That did not seem to impress my hon. friend from Calgary at all. It did not seem to make any difference to him that, as a result of that inquiry, there was a great improvement in the class of boots furnished to the soldiers. My hon. friend said that the Canadian boot manufacturers had lost large amounts of money by reason of that investigation, and that therefore it ought never to have taken place. When my right hon. friend the Prime Minister proposed, that investigation, and himself moved for the committee in this House, it is a wonder that my hon. friend from Calgary did not rise in his place and tell the Prime Minister that, in moving for an investigation while the war was on, he was like the owner of a house whose house was on five stopping to inquire as to the cost of the hose. The same argument would have been as applicable to that case as to this.
When the inquiry was being held by the Committee on Public Accounts with reference to the purchase of horses, why did the hon. gentleman not rise in his place in the committee and say: Now is not the time to investigate with regard to horses; if it goes abroad that poor horses have been bought for the use of the British or Canadian soldiers, the impression will be entertained across the water that Canadian horses are no good, and money will be lost to the farmers of Canada. Better, according to the hon. gentleman, that they should go on selling those old horses at prices in many cases three times what they were worth, than that there should be an investigation, and that the facts should become public. I wonder what my friend, the former member for Kings, Nova 'Scotia, thinks of the speech which my hon. friend made. His regret must be that the hon. gentleman had not spoken out a year or more ago, when it was proposed to investigate the purchase of horses. He might have saved the former member for Kings his seat in this House, and the right hon. the Prime Minister the painful duty, as the result of the investigation in the Public Accounts Committee, of reading the member for Kings out of the party.
And what about binoculars and bandages? They are necessary for the carrying on of the war. When the committee began to investigate the question of binoculars and bandages, why did my hon. friend from Calgary not get up, and, in eloquent and
stentorian tones, such as he and only he can use, say: "Stop, the war is on; you are like the man whose house is burning, and who stops to inquire into the cost or quality of the hose; stop, the Empire is at war, thousands upon thousands of young men are sacrificing their lives upon the battlefields in the defence of the country, and all the energies of our people ought to be directed towards bringing this war to a successful issue: why stop to investigate boots, binoculars, horses and all such trivial matters? leave these questions, for Heaven's sake, leave them till after the war is over, and do not allow any investigation * for fear that the good name of Canada will in some way be brought to the dust." That is the argument which my hon. friend used, the only argument which he presented to this House.
What about the Davidson Commission? What a dreadful thing it must have been in the opinion of my hon. friend from Calgary, to have the evidence brought out- in regard to the purchase of horses in Ontario, which had the deplorable result that a member of the legislature was compelled to resign his seat, and, when he went back to the people for re-election, they refused to declare their confidence in him and elected his opponent by a very large majority. What a grave injustice, in the eyes of my hon. friend, was done to that gentleman, and what a grave wrong was done to the country because that investigation took place when the war was on.
Then, with regard to submarines, with regard to those great war vessels which, according to the cablegrams from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Chilian Government found themselves unable to accept and take over? What about those great war vessels for which thirty or forty per cent more was paid than ought to have been paid? What a terrible wrong was done by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister when he appointed Sir Charles Davidson to investigate the purchase of the submarines. Word might go to England, and even to Germany, to our enemies, according to my hon. friend, that we were really questioning, that we in Canada had found it necessary to question, the utility of those submarines, and the interest of those who had been engaged in (the purchase of them. What a terrible injury, according to my hon. friend, was done to the people of Canada and to the Empire by the investigation which Sir Charles Davidson conducted.

What did my hon. friend from Calgary, in the very height of his eloquence, and with the most profound seriousness, say? What statement did he make to this House, based upon his inner knowledge, upon his trips across the Atlantic, upon his close *association with the members of this Government? He said:
Sir, I have a profound conviction that when this war is over and when an investigation into its conduct has been held alike in the Mother Country and in the overseas dominions, some reputations that are now looked upon as great will fall. I have a profound conviction, too, that men who have proflted by the necessities of the state; who have washed their hands in blood money, so to speak-they and their children's children-will be remembered with execrations and curses by the men who come after.
Serious words, these, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that when my hon. friend used these words he either said too much .or too little. If my hon. friend, with his *close and intimate knowledge of what has *been going on since the war broke out, with his close association with ministers, knows of men now standing high in the councils of the country, or having a high reputation, whose reputation will fall when the war is over-if my hon. friend knows of men who have taken advantage of, and proflted by, the necessities of the State, who have " washed their hands in blood money, so to speak," and who, " with their children's children, will be remembered with execrations and curses by the men who come after them," surely it rests upon my hon. friend as a member of this House, as one who represents the people of this country, to disclose to this Parliament what he knows with reference to those men who are profiting by the war, and " washing their hands in blood money, so to speak." My hon. friend ought not to wait until the war is over in order to expose the wrong-doing which he has reason to know exists to-day. He should come out in the open, and tell this House and the people of this country what he knows with reference to those wrong-doings.
Now, my hon. friend has made a most serious statement which he would not have made if he had not had knowledge of that whereof he speaks. He says:
But now is not the time, in the midst of this great conflict, to cease our activities, to wear out our energies beating against the rock.
I am not able to see any reason why we should wait until the war is over. I do not see why we should not investigate these matters now, and I think the people expect us to investigate them now. No
[Mr. Pugsley.j
harm was done to this country, no harm was done to the Empire, military activities were in no way interfered with, war preparations were in no way impeded, when the investigation into boots took place. When the investigation into charges concerning binoculars, bandages, drugs and submarines took place, no harm was done to this country, and military activities were in no way impeded. I am not able to see what injury would possibly be caused to Canada or the Empire by an investigation into the matters which have been brought before the House with respect to the purchase of shells and other munitions of war.
How could any injury be done? There would be no stoppage of the manufacture of munitions. The manufacture of munitions has now been entrusted to the Imperial Munitions Board. The old Shell Committee did not die a natural death; it was put to death by representatives of the British Government who came to Canada to investigate its conduct. The new Imperial Munitions Board can go on with the work just the same whether this investigation takes place or whether it does not.
Then, my hon. friend says, that the managers of factories and of various industrial establishments would be brought to Ottawa and be kept dancing around for weeks perhaps, and that their industries would be neglected. There is no need of that. It is proposed that a small committee shall be appointed, a majority of whom would be representative of hon. gentlemen opposite. That committee, I take it, would carry on its work in a reasonable and proper manner, and in such a way as to suit the convenience of the various witnesses who would be required. The inquiry would not take a very great while and I am unable to see how there would be any great inconvenience to those who would be summoned as witnesses, or how the work of manufacturing munitions, or the work of the Imperial Munitions Board, would be interfered with. But, surely, when these charges have been made, chargee which have startled the people of the country who are not able to believe it possible that the business of the Empire, which has 'been entrusted to the Government of Canada, is being 5 p.m. carried on in such a reckless and improper manner, and that these vast eums of money are being taken out of the taxpayers of the United Kingdom and of Canada, the fact that a few people may be temporarily inconvenienced by being brought here as witnesses, ought

not to prevent this Parliament from doing its duty and having an investigation into these important matters.
I do not think I need answer more fully the arguments which my hon. friend from Calgary has made, because, as I have said, he does not pretend to question the accuracy of the figures presented by my hon. friend from Carleton. He simply puts his argument against an investigation upon the ground that it in some way or other might interfere with the work of the Imperial Munitions Board and with the military operations to which the Government is attending. I had almost forgotten that the hon. gentleman eaid that this Government were overweighted with great responsibilities and that it would be a cruel thing to place this extra burden upon them. I admit that the right hon. the Prime Minister has grave responsibilities resting upon him, and I admit that the Minister of Militia and Defence has grave responsibilities resting upon him and that his work would necessarily be increased. I think probably also that the Minister of Finance has added responsibilities of a grave character; but how about the others? How about my genial friend the Minister of Public Works? No matter how much he might pretend to be worried by responsibilities connected with the war, he could not make me believe that he really was worried in the slightest degree. His work has not been added to. His work is not one-tenth what it was before the war. If ' what he says is correct, and I do not desire to question what he says, he is only carrying out existing contracts as to which everything of a preliminary character has been done, as to which the plans and specifications were all prepared long ago, and as to which the contractors, under the supervision of the department, are simply carrying out the works to completion. What is to hinder the Minister of Public Works, able man as he is, from giving attention to an investigation of this important subject? What about the Solicitor General? Has the fact that he has been recently elevated to cabinet rank added to his duties, burdens, or responsibilities? I do not think so. What about the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who has lately added a large number of lawyers to his staff to enable him to attend to the law business of the country? If any additional burdens have to be borne, the Minister of Justice takes care to bring lawyers from a distance to Ottawa for the
purpose of bearing them, and he pays them good fat retainers at the expense of the people of this country. I cannot imagine that the war would prevent him from giving personal attention to the examination of these questions. What about the members of the Government without portfolio who belong to the class that we down in the province of New Brunswick call the forecastle members of the Government? They have no important duties to attend to. What about the Secretary of State. He is an able lawyer, or an able notary public; 1 have no doubt that he would be able to give some attention to this investigation, to see that matters were considered properly, and that the truth was fully and plainly brought out by the committee without any bad feeling or any inconvenience to anybody. What about the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of Minister of Mines and Inland Revenue? His work has not been increased'by reason of the war. Then, there is the Minister of Labour, who says' ir. the most positive way that while this war is on he has a feeling of uncertainty as to whether we are going to win or not, that we ought not to consider any social questions, and that we ought not to consider the question of whether we should engage upon a system of technical educr tion because, I suppose, the benefits of these things might pass over to the Germans in case they should conquer the Empire and take Canada. The Minister of Labour says: Hold, stand still, while the war is on. Surely, under those circumstances he would have plenty of time for an investigation into these ques

tions. There may be otheT members of the Government in the same position. Oh, yes, there is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He has not had grave responsibilities, because, very early in the war, he took all the pains he could to put all his war vessels out of commission so that he would not have anything to do, and so that there would not be any responsibility resting on his shoulders. He thought the best thing to do was to leave the trade routes to be guarded by the warships of the Mother Country, and of Australia, and of Japan. Certainly it was the easier way, and it relieved him of a great deal of responsibility, so that I think he will agree with me that he would have plenty of time to work on this committee if it should be appointed. Surely the argument raised by my hon. friend from Calgary that we ought not to add to the burdens and respon-

siibilities of this Government in war time is not a very strong one, and is not calculated to impress this House or this country, and surely the appeal, -which the hon. gentleman made to us that, above all, we should hot obtrude into public questions at the present time what might seem to be partisan matters, ought not to prevail. Let me say to my hon. friend from Calgary that we do not approach this question in any partisan spirit; but if criticism on the part of an Opposition of wrongdoing or improper expenditure of the public money is an evidence of partisanship, we plead guilty, because ever since the commencement of the war, we thought we had a right to take the Prime Minister at his word when, [DOT] upon the occasion of his asking us to vote to the Minister of Finance .all the moneys he might require for the purpose of carrying on the. war, he told us that he would afford us an opportunity of investigating into all public expenditures while the war was on.
