But if that is to be the dividing line between us and hon. gentlemen opposite; if they say that the lid must be kept down until the war is over; if they are to be allowed to say that there will be no examination into public expenditures until then, we, on the other hand, say that we, as the representatives of the people, have a right to demand an investigation into the expenditure of public money. If that is to be the dividing line, then we are willing to admit that we cannot agree with hon. gentlemen opposite, and we are content to' be classed as partisans. My hon. friends opposite, taking the position which they do, must, of course, choose for themselves the word1 which will properly describe their attitude, but the people of this country will have no difficulty in finding language which will fittingly describe it.
My hon. friend from Calgary also urges that there is a grave constitutional question involved in this resolution, and that we cannot properly or constitutionally investigate the expenditure of these moneys until an item appears in the Public Accounts; in other words, until the Minister of Finance and the British Government [Mr. Pugsley.J
make an adjustment of the accounts as between the two countries and, the amount that we pay appears in the Auditor General's Beport. That was not the view taken by the Prime Minister when, in 1903, he voted for a resolution proposed by the Hon. Mr. Monk, one of the greatest constitutional lawyers Canada has ever produced, a . gentlemen who occupied a high position at the bar in his native province, and who was also a distinguished professor of law in Laval University. He took the view and pressed it home strongly that this Parlia ment would not be discharging its duty ir it did not investigate the purchases mad-' for the British Government during the Boer war, and, when the question came lip for decision, the Prime Minister, who i? also a very able constitutional lawyer, felt, constrained to vote for the resolution, as did all his followers, and when the genera1 elections came the charge was made by the right hon. gentleman's friends that the Liberal party had sought to prevent an investigation into the purchases which were made for the British Govern ment at that time. The people, in 1911, tooK the view that the Liberal party was no longer worthy of the confidence of the majority of the people and the present Prime Minister and his party were returned to power. Are they to go back now on the record which they made for themselves in 1903? They are in charge of the affairs of this country to-day; are they to be allowed to say: Although we believed in the position which we took in 1903, yet to-day, because we are in office; because we want to keep the lid down and prevent the people from knowing what is taking place, we are going to vote against any investigation and against the facts getting before the public. That apparently is the position which my right hon. friend is taking; it is the position which my hon. friend from Calgary has pressed him to take; but now that I have complied with his request and have submitted this charge in a form which certainly my right hon. friend can understand and which every man in this country who can read will understand, I hope that he will not adhere to the views which he has presented to the House, or act upon the request of the hon. member for Calgary.
But, the hon. member for Calgary says: Oh, this was not Canadian money at all and we have no right to investigate the expenditure of it. I think we may deal with this question from two standpoints:

one that these shells are being purchased with Canadian money by a partnership consisting of the United Kingdom and of Canada. We have the statement made bv my hon. friend the Minister of Finance early in the session in answer to an inquiry which * I presented to him, that under an arrangement come to between the British Government and the Canadian Government, every dollar expended in connection with the Canadian Expeditionary Forces shall be paid by Canada. This is the statement of the Minister of Finance as reported on page 42 of Hansard:
In a general way, I may say to my hon. friend that the Government of Canada is bearing the entire expense of Canada's participation in the war. There will necessarily be certain accounts which cannot be adjusted until the war is over, or until a later date. .. .
Mr. Pugsley: That means, of course, all the ammunition, all the guns, all the boots and shoes, and all the clothing used by the Canadian soldiers at the front?
*
Sir Thomas White: ... In other words, we desire to pay the entire cost of the Canadian Expeditionary Force abroad.
That includes the cannon, the rifles and the shells which are used by the Canadian soldiers. Therefore, so far as Canada's money is concerned, though the United Kingdom pays for these shells in the first place, a proportion is charged to Canada, the adjustment of the exact amount Canada is to pay being postponed to a later date. What difference does it make whether we pay ten millions or twenty millions now or whether we agree to pay the Mother Country as soon as the accounts are adjusted. From the statement of the Prime Minister it further appears that for the purpose of carrying out this arrangement in good faith, Canada to-day is financing the British Government during the purchase of these munitions of war in Canada. The Prime Minister's statement, on page 30 of Hansard, reads:
I believe that of all the payments to be made during the present month of January, the Canadian Government is providing at least one-half so that we are not only doing our part in producing these munitions of war, but we are also doing our part in temporarily financing for the British Government about one-half of the payments.
The effect of the statement of the Minister of Finance is that these purchases are made and from time to time there will be an adjustment of the accounts as between the British Government and the Canadian Government, and Canada will recognize her liability for her portion. I defy any
hon. gentleman to show that there is a difference between the case as it is and the case as it would be if Canada w'ere to give her own cheques immediately upon these shells going into the possession of the British Government.
But even if that were not the case, the members of this Shell Committee are the appointees of the Minister of Militia, a member of this Government, for whose actions the whole Government is responsible. I notice a disposition on the part of some hon. members to dissociate the Minister of Militia from other members of the Government. I notice especially that when they speak of Colonel Allison, they try to associate the Minister of Militia with Col. Allison. But if the Minister of Militia is associated, rightly or wrongly, with Col. Allison in the purchase of munitions, every member of this Government is equally associated with him.' That is the constitutional principle; that for every act of every member of the Government every other member of the Government is responsible just as if he performed that act himself.
I submit, and I shall be able to prove it, if it is not already proven to your satisfaction, Sir, and to that of members of the House: that the members of this Shell Committee were the appointees of the Minister of Militia. I was indeed surprised when the Prime Minister sought to convey the impression that all that the Minister of Militia had done was to name eight or ten men and to submit those names for the approval of the British Goverftment. I was surprised that my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) should follow the Prime Minister in that idea. There is not one word in the record, or in the correspondence, or in the testimony available to the House, to show that the Shell Committee were the appointees of the British Government; but there is evidence of an overwhelming character to prove that that committee were the appointees of this Government, and of this Government alone. As evidence on that point, we have first the statement made by the Minister of Militia and reported at page 295 of Hansard:
I now come to a very interesting part of the discussion, namely, the Shell Committee. And here let me frankly admit to the House that it is my baby; I am the father of the concern, be it for good or he it for bad, and I purpose sticking to it as long as it has a button left on its jacket.	.
I would like to say to the Minister of Militia that the place in which to stick to the Shell Committee is not on the sunny

beaches or in the shade of the sheltering palms of Florida, but it is in this House, in this Parliament of the nation, and in sight of the people of this country-that is the place in which the Minister of Militia should stand by his " babyhe should not have gone away and left his "baby" to the fate which will befall it. As further evidence, we have the statement in the report prepared by Colonel Carnegie to be signed by General Bertram, and read by the Prime Minister in this House, as appears at page 1570 of Hansard. The Government cannot repudiate that report, because they themselves submitted it for the information of this House. In that report it is stated:
The executive work of the committee has been very wisely entrusted to the chairman. Colonel Bertram, who reports weekly to the Minister of Militia and also to the committee when it meets (which is usually monthly) or more often, at the call of the minister.
There you have the official statement that the committee reports weekly to the Minister of Militia and that it meet's subject to the minister's call, as at the call of an honorary chairman. We have also the letter from Mr. Hichens, who represented the British Government, and who was entrusted with what, I suppose, must have been the unpleasant task of disorganizing this Shell Committee and providing for the appointment of an Imperial Munitions Board to take its place.
I ask hon. members to listen to the words of Mr. Hichens in the letter written to'the Prime *Minister and by him submitted to this House on the 7th instant, for the purpose of giving it knowledge of the position in which matters stood. In his letter to the Prime Minister, which may be found on page 1581 of Hansard, Mr. Hichens says':
In order to carry out your wishes and to make it clear that the purchasing- agency is administratively independent of the Canadian Government, the members of the existing Shell Committee have tendered their resignations to the Minister of Militia, by whom they were appointed.
Consider for a moment what was desired. When Mr. Thomas and Mr. Hichens came to Canada it was desired that this purchasing agency should be kept administratively independent of the Canadian Government. Is that not a statement, as strong as xa statement can be, that the old Shell Committee was not administratively independent of the Canadian Government? Is that not a statement as strong as language could make it, that the old Shell Committee was in reality a branch of this Government, appointed by the Minister of Militia, and

acting for the Minister of Militia and for this Government? In order that the administration of the purchasing agency should Ibe separated from this Government it was required that the Shell Committee should resign and that a new board, to be called the Imperial Munitions Board, and to be appointed by the Imperial Government, should take its place. Mr. Hichens says that the object of the change was to make it clear that the administration of affairs connected with purchases should be altogether independent of the Canadian Government. Listen to the words of Mr. Hichens:
The members of the existing Shell Committee have tendered their resignations to the Minister of Militia, by whom they were appointed, and a new board entitled the " Imperial Munitions Board " has been constituted by the British Minister of Munitions as from November 30, 1915.
In other words, this committee, which was administratively a branch of the Canadian Government; which was administratively attached to the Department of Militia; which reported weekly to the Min-about once a month or oftener at the call about once a month or oftener at the call of the Minister of Militia-this Shell Committee, as Mr. Hichens says, resigned to the Minister of Militia, by whom they were appointed, and a new committee called the Imperial Munitions Board was constituted by the British Minister of Munitions as from Nov. 30, 1915. This shows as clearly as it can be shown, that in order that the Shell Committee appointed by the Minister of Militia should be done away with and a new board appointed by the Imperial Minister of Munitions, the members of the Shell Committee were required to resign. They promptly resigned to the Minister of Militia, and a new board was appointed by the Imperial Minister oif Munitions to take their_ place. I do not see how it is possible for me to present any stronger evidence than that that the Shell Committee was the appointee of the Minister of Militia and, accordingly, of the Canadian Government.
Sir, what further argument is there for an investigation, altogether apart from the question of the appointment of the Shell Committee? It is said by gentlemen opposite that the British Government requested the Minister of Militia to name a committee. Granting for a moment that that was all that the British Ministry did, surey that was entrusting an important matter to the

Canadian Minister of Militia. Surely in a most important matter the British Government were relying on him to select the men to do this work. The Minister of Militia names these * men and they go on and make purchases. They waste the money of Great Britain to the extent of millions of dollars; waste it to an amount not less than $80,000,000, as we allege, and more likely to upwards of $100,000,000. Surely the Minister of Militia has the right to investigate the manner in which these men whom he named have discharged their duties. But, Sir, the Minister of Militia was asked to name this committee not because he was Major-General Sir Sam Hughes, but because he occupied the important position of Minister of Militia. He was in that respect, as in all other respects, the trustee of the people of 'Canada. The honour of the people of Canada was entrusted to his keeping and to the keeping of his colleagues in the Government. 'The people of Canada to-day demand an investigation as to how these men named by the Minister of Militia have discharged the sacred trust which was vested in them. It is no use trying to balk this inquiry by technicalities. The people of Canada are saying to-day, that in respect of this vast expenditure of money they have a right to know the facts. Hon. gentlemen on the other side say: Oh, the British Government have not asked for an inquiry. Sir, there is something else besides the mere wish of Mr. Hichens or of other gentlemen who are connected with the British Government. As I have said, the honour and the good name of Canada are involved in this matter. In view of the facts which have been presented by the hon. member for Oarleton, the people have the right to have this matter investigated by Parliament; they have the right to ascertain the facts with reference to these grave charges; they have the right to be informed by sworn testimony as to whether any answer can be made to these apparently unanswerable charges. If any answer can be given they have a right to know what that answer is.
The hon. member for Calgary says: you are seeking to besmirch the honour and good name of the manufacturers of Canada. Sir, I deny that. We have not on this side of the House made a single charge against any manufacturer in this country. It has not been suggested, and it cannot be proved that the manufacturers of Canada have combined to raise the prices to the
Shell Committee; it has not been suggested and it cannot be proved that they ever demanded any fixed price for the manufacture of these munitions of war. The evidence is that the 'Shell Committee themselves voluntarily fixed the prices and gave to the manufacturers the prices which they so fixed. The simple question for the manufacturers was as to whether, at the prices fixed by the Shell Committee, they were willing to fill the orders offered to them. I repudiate, therefore, as absolutely without a shadow of foundation the statement that we are seeking to besmirch the good name of the manufacturers of this country, or to impeach their honour in any way.
In answer to the charges made, the Government talk about what has been done by our soldiers who have gone to the front; they talk of the splendid bravery which our men have displayed, the noble manner in which they have been willing to lay down their lives for the Empire. According to these hon. gentlemen, the braver our boys are on the battlefield the greater can be the bungling and boodling at home. That is apparent from the argument of these gentlemen, because that is the only excuse they offer for this dreadful waste of public money. You will remember, Sir, that when the Minister of Militia addressed the House that was the only answer he had to the charges which the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) and I ventured to put before the House in the debate on the Address. We have made grave charges against the members of the Shell Committee and against the Minister of Militia, and necessarily against the Government by reason of the Minister of Militia being a member of this Government. Putting the charges in concrete form, what is alleged? In thesfirst place it is alleged:
That the Shell Committee fixed excessive and unreasonable prices for shells and other munitions and goods to be furnished to the British Government, which by arrangement between the British Government and the Canadian Government were to be paid for in part by Canada.
Is that not absolutely true? Is it not absolutely true that these munitions were to be paid for partly by the British Government and partly by Canada? Can anybody doubt that it is true that the Shell Committee fixed excessive and unreasonable prices for shells and other munitions, and goods to be furnished to the British Government? Sir, I say it is true. I defy any member in this House to combat the figures, and the arguments resulting from them,

which have been submitted by the hon. member for Carleton. They are absolutely unanswerable. The Minister of Militia did not-shall I say dare not-venture to remain here in this House for the purpose of answering them. He knew what the charges . were before he left, and he did not venture to remain in this House for the purpose of attempting to give an answer. The hon. member for Carleton gave the dates of these various orders and he showed beyond question that at the very time that this Shell Committee were giving orders to small companies, mushroom companies, at prices which the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) says were sufficiently high to cover the cost of the plant, they were giving large orders at the same prices to established concerns which had already been paid many times over the cost of their plant, and which received in that way enormous profits from the orders which were so given to them. That is the statement we make. We not only make it, but we substantiate it by the facts; and, Sir, upon my responsi'bilty as a member of this House, and knowing the grave consequences which would necessarily fall on me if" I should fail to make good the charges which have been made, I declare that this charge is true. I declare that the Shell Committee did fix excessive and unreasonable prices for shells and other munitions. The next charge, put in concrete form, is:
That such prices were fixed without competition and were far in excess of what would necessarily have been paid if ordinary business methods had been pursued.
Is there any doubt about that? Did any one of the hon. gentlemen opposite, from my hon. friend the Minister of Militia down to the hon. member for Calgary, pretend that the Shell Committee asked for competitive prices?
Was not every price, in every instance, for every class of munitions, fixed by the Imperial Government before the contracts were awarded?
I would say, no.
That would settle the whole question.

I have no information that it was. But suppose it were so-and I have yet to learn it was so-'but suppose it were so, is that any justification for these men -who were upon the spot allowing the British treasury to be robbed by the giving of these excessive prices? We have heard it said that these British officials had no
idea of the possibilities of manufacturing shells and other munitions of war in Canada. We have been told stories of the amazing stupidity and want of knowledge of Canada on the part of officials of the British Government. I do not wonder at that when we find that the Prime Minister never, apparently, had sufficient faith in the resources of Canada to stand up and tell some of these British officials that they had a very inadequate knowledge of the resources of Canada when they put forward their statements as to what Canada could do and as to what Canada could not do. I say, Sir, we do know that the Shell Committee, in many cases, gave to these big firms-many of them companies in which they were largely interested, and of which they themselves were directors, in some of which they were the managing heads and the controlling factors-practically the same enormous prices which they gave to other small companies engaged in the manufacturing business. And when we show that these companies have made millions and millions beyond what would naturally have been paid if ordinary business methods had been pursued; when these prices were fixed not by the British Government, but by the appointees of this Government through the Minister of Militia, are we to be told that because the British Government officials, 3,000 miles away, having no knowledge of the industrial possibilities of Canada, knowing nothing pt our great factories, or of our skilled workmen, not believing it was possible that Canada could do as much in the way of manufacturing as the people of any other country in the world, and do it as quickly; is it any excuse or answer to the charge we make as to these enormous prices being paid, to say: Oh, well, the British Government did not complain; they did not object to the prices which the Shell Committee fixed, and, therefore, no matter what was paid we have no right to investigate.
Will the hon. member be good enough to specify what company he refers to whose managing head and controller was on the committee and which got large contracts at excessive prices?

Mr. Speaker, I purpose devoting a very short time to some remarks on the question of shells, and then I will proceed to discuss the question of fuses, and in connection with that I purpose reading to the House a communication which I have received from Colonel Carnegie, a member of the Shell Committee, and which I deem if only right and just to him to read to the House, because he has expressed a desire that I should do so.
With regard to shells, there has been an effort made by the Minister of Militia and others to convince the House that the making of shells was a matter attended with very great difficulty and that it was almost impossible to induce Canadian manufacturers to engage in the. work. It is interesting to compare the statements which the Minister of Militia and other hon. gentlemen opposite have made at different times. The right hon. Prime Minister made 'an extraordinary statement with regard to the manufacture of shells. He has told this House that almost ever since he and his colleagues came into office they had the feeling that there was danger oif war between Germany and the British Empire. He stated probably a year ago

When the Prime Minister and his far-seeing businesslike colleagues, gentlemen with business acumen, heard that there was likely to be war, would you not have thought that, if they had a reasonable regard for the interests of the country, they would have looked into the question of what Canada could do in the way of making munitions? Did their vision never go beyond the sending of our men to take their places in the batfle line? Did they not think of shells, guns, rifles, explosives? Does it not seem incredible to you, Mr. Speaker, that a month after the war had broken out the Prime Minister had doubts as to whether shells could be made in Canada in any large quantities? One would almost think that the Prime Minister had been asleep during the fifteen or eighteen years of Canada's wonderful prosperity, One would think that he was oblivious to the fact that great industries had been created during those years; that marvellous strides in the way of industrial development had been made, and that, when war broke out, as has since been demonstrated, Canada, in proportion to her population, was better equipped for carrying on manufacturing of any kind or description than any

other country in the world. These gentlemen express themselves as amazed at what Canada did, and at what the Canadian manufacturers did, as if they were surprised to learn that Canadian manufacturers are just as skilful, just as energetic, just as resourceful as the manufacturers of any part	of the British

I am sure that that is his wish, because he requests that I should give publicity to .his repudiation of the charge which he thinks 1 preferred against him. The letter is as follows:
Imperial Munitions Board,
Ottawa, February 26, 1916.
Dear Sir,-A few days before leaving- England I received a cutting from the Toronto Star of January 20, in which the following statement was made purporting to be an extract from a speech made by you in the House of Commons, Ottawa, January 19:
"What did General Bertram do after receiving his knighthood which I believe must have been given him as a handy way to get rid of. him? General Bertram declared that he himself and he alone fixed the prices. But he hasn't stated the whole facts. Col. Carnegie was associated with him and these two men distributed favours to their friends and themselves. This was entirely irregular. Millions of dollars have been taken from the British taxpayer by reason of the system."'
I should have passed the matter over as unworthy of notice had it not been raised in Parliament by a responsible member such as yourself with a decided intent to reflect upon my integrity. Whatever prompted you to associate my name with irregular practices I care not, but I cannot allow such statements to pass unrefuted as you have personally attacked me. I not only resent with my whole soul the charges it is reported you made, that I with General 109*
Bertram placed contracts with friends and favourites, but I deny them absolutely.
I have the charity to believe that you have: given utterances to allegations about which you: had no ground for proof and that you have noknowledge of the man whose character you have impeached. Confident of this I give at some length an account of my connection with the committee and demand a public explanation and apology.
If you are in doubt about the character of the man against whom you have launched such charges I would refer you to my records for fifteen years in the Government service at Woolwich Arsenal, for four years at Hadfield's Sheffield, and for four years at Samuel Osborn's, Sheffield, and latter to my career as private consulting engineer in London.
If you will inquire at the various learned societies in England and Scotland; if you will inquire into my social and public work for my fellows in the cities in which I have lived; if you will closely investigate every act of service I have rendered to the .Shell Committee since September, 1914 ; if you will examine the records of all transactions with which I have been engaged; if you will discuss with manufacturers minutely my dealings with them and also inquire of the gentlemen who visited Canada from England with the object of investigating the work of the Shell Committee, I defy you or any other man to find the slightest trace of any irregular practice of conscious wrongdoing in any work with which I have been connected and with any part of the committee's work I have handled.
I have received words of appreciation from Lord Kitchener and the personal thanks of Mr Lloyd George in connection with my services on the -Shell Committee.
I came to Canada at the beginning of the war a comparative stranger. I have laboured incessantly not only in connection with the work of the Shell Committee but with a view to the industrial development of the country and I believe I have the confidence of the Prime Minis-teL. Sir Robert Borden, and the Minister of Militia, General Sir Sam Hughes, who have closely followed the work I have done in connection with the committee.
Reference has been made to my connection with a Welland company. About four years ago I visited Canada with the object of investigating how far the steel manufacturing industry could be developed in the country and I ultimately decided with other friends to start steel manufacture in Welland by utilizing the cheap electric power obtained in the district. I invested my own capital and induced others in England to invest theirs. Being an expert in steel manufacture, I was appointed a director of, and consulting engineer to the company, and at my office in London designed the works which were ultimately completed just before the war broke out. Instead of taking the usual consulting fees such as I received from clients for whom I was doing similar work in Britain and the continent, I decided to accept payment over a period of five years so that the company would not at the outset be taxed unduly, f did this because the company had difficulty in raising capital in Canada which the Canadian directors fully expected to oh'tin.
I arrived in Canada tow? j the end of September, 1914, with the obj' f starting up the new works. Before my ai ,al the Shell Committee was formed, an order was placed with the Welland Company for shells, and the first price to be paid was already fixed.

I had no knowledge whatever that a Shell Committee had been formed or that shells were to be made in Canada, until after I arrived. I wish to emphasize this fact as it has been stated that I was party to the placing of shell contracts with the Welland Company at the high price originally given by the War Office.
Having a thorough knowledge of shell manufacture, being for many years in charge of the various branches in the shell department at Woolwich Arsenal, the attention of General Hughes was drawn to this fact and my services were commandeered right away for three months to instruct Canadian manufacturers in the art of shell making.
As the Welland Company with which I was connected had received an order for shells and my brother, Mr. E. Carnegie, was general manager and also member of the Shell Committee,
I placed my resignation in the hands of the board and also suggested the withdrawal of my capital, notwithstanding the fact that General Hughes and the members of the committee knew my connection with the Weiland Company before my appointment as Ordnance Advisor. My fellow directors would not at first accept my resignation as they stated it would jeopardize the interests of the shareholders who had been induced to place their capital in the company because they knew me and depended upon my expert help in making it a success. They also referred to the agreement I had with the company to give them my services as consulting engineer. Financially it would have been inconvenient at the time to pay me out, but I persisted in resigning immediately from the directorate, stating that I should give to them the same assistance as to any other company engaged in the manufacture of munitions. I stated also that I should withdraw my capital immediately X saw the company was in such a position that I could .sell out without interfering with its success. The company ultimately consented to liberate me from my obligations as their con-suiting engineer, and I have had no financial or other interest in the company since last September.	.
That was September, 1915, a year after the first order was given.
As my term of service with the Shell Committee as Ordnance Advisor was for three months only, X was advised by many of ^ my friends that I was making a needless sacrifice in resigning- my directorship of the Welland company. The committee at that time understood that no more shells would be required, and only a few companies were willing to undertake the work even after a guarantee had been given that any loss , would be made good in the event of the work not paying.
The Welland Company with which I was connected received the orders because of my brother's knowledge of shell manufacture, he being one of the few men In Canada who knew anything about the work.
At the end of three months I returned of England, saw the officials of the War Office, informed them of Canada's ability to produce shells and obtained their permission, after much discussion, to use basic steel in Canada for high explosive shells. This had never been previously granted and meant a very great deal to Canadian steel manufacturers who produced only basic steel. I also induced the War Office to place additional orders for shells in the Dominion.
I was asked by the Shell Committee if I would continue my service qs Ordnance Advisor

without stating any definite period, it being expected that the orders then placed would he completed in the spring. I threw in my lot not knowing how long I would be required to act, and on my return to Canada I had most attractive offers made to me by private companies, the remuneration from which was very many times more than that paid to me by the committee. I mention this fact simply to show that it was not a matter of money with me at all, but the highest sense of duty which impelled me.
While in England it was suggested to me hy Lord Moulton that we should try to manufacture trinitrotoluol in Canada. This was quite a new departure for Canada, and I urged that the matter be taken up with earnestness. Through the efforts of General Hughes and Mr. Plummer, of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Sydney, N.8., plants were erected in less than four months for the production of toluol from the coke oven waste gases which were subsequently trinltrated and shipped to England. To-day several plants are now producing T.N.T. and approximately eight hundred thousand pounds are being produced.
At the suggestion of General Hughes, with the support of Sir Robert Borden, a commission was appointed to investigate the feasibility of refining copper in Canada and producing metallic zinc. I had the honour to ;be chairman of the commission on which Professor Stansfield, of McGill University, and Dr. Wilson, of the Mines Branch, gave most valuable assistance in accomplishing the end we had in view, and today both zinc and copper are being refined in Canada. I have striven to encourage the development of Canada's manufactures to include every possible material required for the complete round of ammunition. At the beginning of the war we were dependent entirely upon the States or England for many of our materials. To-day all classes of material required are now being manufactured in Canada. Some of the new industries established will become permanent in the supply of domestic requirements hitherto imported These facts alone are of more value to me than all the thanks and praise that man can give.
I just pause here to remark that the Minister of Militia led us to understand that the use of basic steel was entirely-owing to his original thought on the subject; but Col. Carnegie appears tcj claim that he is entitled to credit for that suggestion.
Last April General Sir Sam Hughes added my name to the list of members of the committee, an honour which I esteemed highly, particularly as it was unsought. During my whole connection with the Shell Committee, before I was a member and since I was appointed a member, it has always been a pleasure to work along with General Bertram and the other members of the committee. General Bertram and I were virtually the executive for many months together, until latterly when the work of the committee increased Mr. Riddell was appointed financial advisor.
During these months of incessant work from early morning until midnight, I have bad the pleasure of meeting many talented Canadians, whose ability, energy and charms I have coveted. I can say without the shadow of doubt that in all my associationes with the Canadian Shell Committee and the many manufacturers

with whom I have had the pleasure of doing business, I have not detected any sugest.ion of what is known in Canada as " Graft " or crookedness. Had I, as a stranger to Canada, believed that the men of business were soaked in habits contrary to the laws of morality such as some writers to the press would suggest, I would despair of seeing Canada that great and industrial asset of the Empire which I have not only dreamed it will become, but to which end I have worked with my whole strength.
While in England, from which I have just returned, I have been on, Canada's business working with constant diligence in securing additional orders for shells and materials, the details of which are well known to the ministry there.
I have written at length as a strong protest [DOT]and an' emphatic denial of the imputations made upon my integrity. I shall be the last to admit that in an organization such as the Shell Committee, which in the course of a year grew from a small institution to one of the most responsible in Canada, no mistakes were made in dealing with the many-sided problems which faced us. The wonder to me is that many more mistakes were not made. When the mistakes of the Shell Committee are compared with the mistakes made by similar organizations at home one xs amazed to find anywhere in Canada a discordant note regarding the work rendered by a body of men who gave their services so will-ir.gly during the Empire's struggle.
I remain, sir,
Yours vefy truly,

Ottawa.

I have nothing for which to apologize to Colonel Carnegie. I am very glad indeed to do him full and complete justice as far as I can by placing upon Hansard the two letters which he has written to me. They state his position and it will be for the public to judge whether or not there has been any intentional slandering of him or any intentional impeachment of his honour on my part. I am not conscious of having done anything for which I should apologize, and I have nothing to retract from my remarks in my speech on the Address. There is nothing in Colonel Carnegie's letter to detract from the statement I then made, and which I repeat: that the members of the Shell Committee were directors, and in some instances the directing force, of companies which received orders for vast quantities at prices far and away beyond what was reasonable and fair. That is the important statement which I made in the debate on the Address and that is the important statement which I make to-night; that these gentlemen were in effect both buyers and sellers, and that as buyers they fixed the prices at which they would buy from the companies of which they were themselves the directors, which prices were far and away beyond what was fair and reasonable, that is the criticism which I make with regard to members of the Shell Committee. I do not charge them in that respect with fraud, I do not charge them in that respect with criminal intention, but what I do charge is that there was a duty- devolving upon them, a duty devolving upon the Minister of Militia and upon the members 01 this Government which appointed this committee, to see that they discharged the trust reposed in them in a reasonable and businesslike manner. When it is proved in this House-as it is proved by the figures presented by the hon. member for Carleton -that in the giving of these orders in a short period extending over some fifteen or eighteen months, there was unnecessarily taken out of the taxpayers of Canada and

of the United Kingdom the enormous sum of upwards of $80,000,000, we have the strongest possible ground for complaining of the unbusinesslike and improper methods that were pursued. I have already said that if the Government of Canada in the exercise of their judgment thought it wise to encourage industry throughout the country and to relieve industrial depression, the aid for that purpose ought to have been taken out of the Canadian treasury and not out of the pockets of the British taxpayers.
But, Sir, the Minister of Finance has been made very comfortable by these enormous war profits. I can well understand, whenever the Prime Minister would hear of these excessive prices, the Minister of Finance saying to him: My dear Premier, don't you worry. The Finance Minister is far-sighted; he is looking forward to the revenue. He said: Don't you worry over the $80,000,000 of excess profits which these war munitions manufacturers may get; I am going to take twenty-five per cent of it back and put it into the Canadian treasury; don't you worry, Sir Eobert. I can imagine the Minister of Finance looking towards the heavens with that beatific smile which covers his face when he is evolving some great and 'beautiful thought, and I can imagine him saying to the Prime Minister: Don't you worry. The Finance Minister has now come down with his taxation measures along these very lines and he proposes to take back twenty-five per cent of the profits which have gone to the manufacturers, and which aTe to be paid jointly by the British treasury and the Canadian treasury. If, as I suppose, the British treasury pays about ninety per cent and the Canadian treasury ten per cent, the Minister of Finance will be in the happy position that while Canada is only paying ten per cent of these excessive profits, he will get back twenty-five per cent and the Canadian treasury will be fifteen per cent to the good when the matter is finally closed. No wonder the Minister of Finance has been during all these months looking forward with happy anticipation to this means of supplementing the revenue. My hon. friend has also made the fact that he is going to impose taxes upon the manufacturers of munitions of war, an excuse for presenting it as a system of taxation and exacting taxes from the general business interests. He thinks he will be able now to say to the people: You cannot complain, because, as you see, we are taxing the war profits.
I would have supposedi that there were two or three plain duties devolving upon this Government and upon the Shell Committee. One, to get munitions of war at the lowest possible price, and another to carry out in good faith the assurance which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister had given to the people of Great Biritaw, that Canada was prepared to consecrate her resources to the service of the Empire. If the Government wanted to relieve industrial depression throughout Canada by establishing small manufacturing concerns and giving them small orders for munitions, they should have said to these concerns: You must take these orders at reasonable and fair prices. If the Government found it necessary to bonus them by paying them a price that would cover the cost of plant, they should pay it out of the Canadian treasury, and not out of the pocket of the British taxpayer. I would have thought that that would be the view which the Shell Committee would have taken.
I shall now, in concluding, make reference to the purchase of fuses. There is no question about the truth of the statement which was contained in the speech of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, that there was great and unnecessary delay in the production of the finished shell which has greatly hampered the work of our armies at the front. If hon. gentlemen need any further proof of that, let them read the statement which was published by the Imperial Munitions Board, through Mr. J. W. Flavelle, the chairman, and in which he said that the Shell Committee had gone on making empty shells, and had paid no attention to the question of procuring fuses. He said that it would be a waste of money to continue turning out the empty shells until they could catch up with a supply of fuses. This is the statement, in concrete form, which is made: That the Shell Committee neglected, delayed, and failed to endeavour to provide for the construction in Canada of an adequate supply of fuses; that it proceeded to award to Mr. J. Wesley Allison, on behalf of a foreign corporation, a contract amounting to $22,000,000, and made an advance of $3,750,000; that the making of the contract through Colonel Allison was unwise and improvident, and was entered into with the knowledge and connivance of the Minister of Militia, and that the Shell Committee failed to obtain delivery of the fuses within a reasonable time. That is the charge which I

make and which we can prove if the motion of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is granted. And, Sir, is not that a serious charge to make against this committee and against the Minister of Militia? It is that that committee went outside of Canada to the United States for the purpose of obtaining an article which they could just as easily have obtained in Canada; that they negotiated there through Colonel Allison, giving through him an order for the enormous amount of $22,000,000. Think of it, Sir, $22,000,000 given to two companies who, as I charge, had no plants to enable them to manufacture fuses, and to whom the Shell Committee advanced the enormous sum of $3,750,000 in order to enable them to equip their plants so that they could engage in the manufacture of fuses. Why did they not do that for Canada? Is there any hon. gentleman opposite who will justify the Shell Committee and the Minister of Militia in respect of the giving of this vast order for fuses in the United States under the circumstances which I have mentioned? I pause for a reply. The Minister of Militia has gone away, and he has left here an hon. gentleman who, he says, will lepresent and defend him. I ask that gentleman to rise in his place to-night, if he will venture to do so, and say if he justifies the Shell Committee for giving this order for fuses in the United States. Sir, it cannot be done. The same advance of $3,750,000 to Canadian manufacturers would have secured the manufacture of fuses in this country just as well as such an advance could secure their manufacture in the United States. When I tell you, Sir, that not very long after this, upon the urgent request of a manufacturer in Canada, an order was given at a lower price and for only about half a million fuses, as was shown in the figures presented by my hon. friend from Carleton, N. B. (Mr. Carvell), you will see how utterly unjustifiable was this transaction. While in my speech on the Address I referred to this matter of fuses being ordered in the United States and made some very severe charges against the Shell Committee in respect of them, yet Colonel Carnegie, in the letters which he addressed to me, did not think it worth while to refer to the question of fuses at all, although I am told that Colonel Carnegie, the high-minded gentleman who wrote those letters, is the member of the Shell Committee who is largely responsible for the making, through Colonel J. Wesley Allison, of this improvident contract in the
TMr. Pugsley.]
United States. I am told-I do not know how true it is, but I believe it is the case; I shall be corrected if I am wrong-that those companies have not yet delivered a single fuse, notwithstanding the fact that the order was given a considerable time ago and that the enormous sum of $3,750,000 was advanced to them.	*
Now, Sir, I have taken a somewhat longer time than I expected to take; but the matter is of such importance that it seems to me it is worthy of the time which has been occupied. When in the debate upon the Address I made remarks of a general character, but remarks which I knew would, if necessary, be followed up by the eVidence when my hon. friend from Carleton came to deliver his speech, I hoped that in a matter of such grave importance, and one in which the people of Canada were so deeply interested, the Government would at once have said that the matter should be investigated; and then it would not have been necessary to make these statements to the House, and the facts would not have become public until they were presented before the committee of investigation. But, although I endeavoured to present, in a somewhat cursory way, the evidence which I had, so as to give to the House an idea of what would be proved in case a committee were formed, not treating the matter in any partisan spirit at all, what was the immediate result? My hon. friend the Solicitor General made one of the bitterest speeches which I have ever heard him make-and the hon. gentleman, although he may not feel any bitterness, can assume it. By his speech he sought to arouse all the worst passions existing in the bosoms of hon!. members on the other side of the House; he depicted me as everything that was unpatriotic and unworthy of commendation; and my hon. friends opposite, who usually have a somewhat friendly feeling towards me, seemed on that occasion to be exceedingly changed in their demeanour and almost to feel that I had done something very unworthy of a member of this Parliament.
Oh, no.

In the press of the
country, the course of the Solicitor General was followed, and my hon. friend from Carleton was also charged with doing what was unpatriotic and unworthy.
Oh, no.

We come now to the consideration of the resolution of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), for whom every one has the highest praise, and we ask, in all candour and in tall sincerity, that this expenditure of $380,000,000, in which the people of Canada and the people of Great Britain are interested in proportion to the men whom they will have engaged in battle before this war is over, shall be investigated by a committee to be appointed for that purpose. We do not think that the people of this country will be content to wait, as my hon. friend from Calgary has asked us to do, until the war is over. If there is iany member of this Shell Committee, or any member of this Government, or any one who has been employed by the Shell Committee, who, in the language of my hon. friend from Calgary, has washed his hands in blood money, the people of this country have a right to know that fact now. They ought not to [DOT] be asked to entrust their business longer to men who are guilty in the way my hon. friend from Calgary has described; and it is not to the interest of the people of this country that our only rddress shall be that, as my hon. friend says, their children and their children's children shall be remembered with execrations and curses for the advantage which they have taken of the necessities of the people in this terrible war. We think the investigation ought to be now, because the people are demanding it and will be 'satisfied with nothing less. But, Sir, I cannot believe that hon. gentlemen opposite will be so unwise in their own interest as to refuse so reasonable a request. As I stated at the opening of my remarks, while I think that the charges already made were sufficiently definite, yet, in deference to my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden), who wanted some member of the House to rise in his place and take * the responsibility of putting these charges in concrete form. I have taken upon myself that responsibility. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), I understand, is likely to follow me. If he does,, he may take the technical ground that this motion ought to be dropped and the charge presented in connection with a new and substantive motion. But that would be an objection of the most technical character. The only object of requiring the charge to be made by a member is to relieve the House from frivolous
charges being made for which no member ventures to take the responsibility. Let us deal with matters of substance and not with matters of form. We have heard the evi-[DOT] dence presented by my hon. friend from Carleton; we have the resolution of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, demanding in the name of the people of this country an investigation into the transactions of the Shell Committee; and you have inyself, a humble member of this House, rising in my place in support of the motion, and taking upon myself the full responsibility, as a member of the House, of undertaking to prove these charges.
Mr. Speaker, this Government may ask their supporters to vote down this resolution. They may say to the people of Canada:	"No matter what mismanagement, no matter what waste of money there may have been; no matter how improperly this Shell Committee may have acted; no matter how much knowledge the Minister of Militia may have had of these improper and irregular practices; no matter what the evidence may be, yet we are prepared to vote against allowing the light of day to shine upon these transactions; we are prepared to call upon our supporters to prevent an investigation of this matter." But let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that, although many things have happened during the months which have gone by since we last assembled in Parliament that have tended^ to weaken the confidence of the people in this Administration, no administration that ever existed in this country ever took a course more likely to be universally condemned by the people than will be the course of this Government if they vote against the passing of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I approach the
discussion of this resolution convinced, first of all, that it has not the zealous support even of hon. gentlemen in the minority in this House. I am convinced, furthermore, from observation of the course of the debate, that the heart of the mover himself, the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), is by no means behind the course he has taken. I am not one who can assume, having some knowledge of hon. gentlemen opposite, that there are going to be defections when the formal vote comes. But I am convinced of this, that there are hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, not a few, who realize the position we are in and what this resolution means, and who, if they had the slightest

against the Government, and the Government resigned. Consequently, an investigation, or an attempt at investigation, followed. Those who have read the words of Mr. Gladstone at that time will realize the wisdom and prescience of that statesman in regard to the policy against which he protested and in respect of which he went out of office. He told the Commons of Great Britain that there could be no effective investigation; that any investigation that would be attempted would necessarily prove a farce; that it would do harm at home and produce disaster abroad. He rejoiced that his last words as a member of the Cabinet of the Earl of Aberdeen embodied a solemn protest against a proceeding which in his judgment meant weakness to his own country both at home and abroad. An investigation followed, and if ever there was a fiasco, if ever there was a farce pure and simple- except possibly the speeches to which we sometimes listen in this House from the hon. member for St. John-if ever there was a fiasco, it was the work of that investigating committee. 'Now, to prove just what that committee did and to enter a warning as to what would result should we follow the behests of hon. gentlemen opposite, let me read this from its report:
The difficulty of the task has been enhanced by the impossibility of bringing some persons as witnesses who could have furnished important information. From the same cause some persons are left under imputations in regard to which your committee regret that they can pronounce no conclusive opinion. The fullness of the inquiry has been restricted by considerations of state, so that at the outset of this report your committee must admit that they have heen compelled to end an Inquiry which they have heen unable satisfactorily to complete.
Here we have the admission of the men most favourable to the inquiry, the men who themselves accepted appointments on the committee, that they were unable to produce any adequate results. That was the last time the Government of Great Britain-even although serious charges of a certain nature were made-ever launched a general inquiry such as would expose to the enemy the resources of their country during a war. Do I hear the hon. member for Carleton say they did it in the South African war? Be tried to show the House that they did something, hut what they did was not at all as he described. It was a different thing entirely, in its character and kind, from the resolution we are asked to adopt. It was an entirely different thing in character and kind from the

resolution which carried in 1855, during the Crimean War. What was it that they did during the South African War? According * to the hon.. member for Oarleton they passed in May, 1901, a resolution in the following language:
That a select committee he appointed to consider and report upon any allegations of fraud and irregularity in connection with War Office contracts-
Does the House get the words? "Any allegations of fraud and irregularity." This was passed in May, 1901. Everybody knows what an irregularity is, especially when associated with the name of fraud.
Fraud and irregularity in connection with. War Office contracts during the last 12 months. That the committee have power to send for persons, papers, and records, and that five he a quorum.
At the same time a general inquiry was asked to be set on foot, an inquiry into the entire management of affairs connected with the war, an inquiry into purchases and the like; and that inquiry was refused by the Government of the day and postponed until the conclusion of the war. Why? Because you can inquire into a specific allegation of fraud or irregularity and not expose to the enemy any of the resources of the country. You could not set on foot a general searching inquiry and fail to do harm to the interests of the state.. Consequently anything in the nature of a general inquiry was refused, and refused in - the public interest, until the war was over.
Is there any charge of fraud or irregularity here? , Even were this shell committee, our committee, acting under our instructions, subject to our disposition and our supervision, a committee whose every act we supervised and were responsible-fox; even were it such a committee there is nothing brought forward and nothing urged to bring it within the purview of that British resolution and make-it the duty of this Government to grant an investigation. The hon. member for St. John, not five minutes before he sat down, made it clear to the House that he charged nothing in the way of fraud or irregularity even against the Shell Committee; yet who will ever forget the demeanour and the-language of horror, yes, of tragedy, with which he opened that address? He was going to meet the Prime Minister of the-day, and from his place in Parliament take the whole responsibility for the grave-and serious charges he was going to make; he was going to expose himself to the abdication of his seat in Parlia-

ment, and to the ignominy of his fellow members and the whole of Canada; he was going to make such charges against the Shell Committee and the Minister of Militia, and to take the full responsibility therefor. I congratulate him that he has not lost his sense of the dramatic. His knowledge of stage effect would compare with that of Sheridan himself. But I am afraid he does not judge aright the intelligence of this House, if he thinks that any member of the Parliament of Canada is going to call a thing a charge because he so denominates it. One may, of course, charge the Government and the Conservative party with being inferior in intelligence to the Liberal party and to the Government of the Liberal party, and he might clothe that charge with all th^ habiliments, all the trappings of great importance, and so endeavour to convince the public that he was making something in the nature of a charge involving the honour of a minister of the Crown. But surely he cannot so deceive the Commons of this country.
What has he done? Let us throw off some of the dressings; let us throw off some of the verbiage, and get down to the meat. Let us see what " charge " he actually does make against this Government, in respect of which he takes such a fearful responsibility on himself, a responsibility almost unprecedented in the history of Parliament, occurring only once in ten or twelve years, and by making which " charge " he places his own seat and his own reputation at stake.
He charges that we have a Shell Committee appointed by this Government. Surely it is appointed by this Government. In that respect the charge is true; he takes no risk in making that statement, because we have plainly stated so for over a year.
He charges that prices were fixed without competition, and were far in excess of what would necessarily be paid if ordinary business methods had been pursued, and, therefore, there have been wasted large sums of money, conservatively estimated at at least $80,000,000, which will be improperly taken from the people of the United Kingdom and of Canada. That is a charge all right; but I have sat in Parliament, I think, almost every day for seven years, and I do not think I ever sat here a day when I did not hear that charge, or some exactly similar charge, made on the floor of this House, that the Government had expended money where they should not have expended money, that they had paid too much for this or for that or for the other thing. Who
ever heard of an Opposition that was not charging that every day of its existence?
Then, he says that they gave large orders at excessive prices and without competition to companies in which members of the committee were largely interested, and of some of which companies members of the said committee were the directing heads. Is that a charge of fraud? He knows better than to call it so himself. He knows that, under the law of this country and of every country, even if what he says has a vestige of truth, you can deal with an incorporated company entirely irrespective of whether or not you yourself hold stock in it.
Furthermore, he charges that there has been great and unnecessary delay in the furnishing of completed shells for the use of Canadian and British forces at the front. Why, the Minister of Munitions in Great Britain admits that on behalf of the British Government. Is that a charge involving the honour of a Government?
Let me go a little further. Here is the most amusing thing of all: that the Shell Committee neglected and delayed, for an undue period of time, to provide the fuses necessary to render the shells effective. One would really think that we were firing off our shells in France without any fuses in them. One would think that we did not know that there had to be a fuse to fire a shell. As if those could not be made anywhere else than here, and as if in the arrangement at the War Office, involving, as it did, the whole of the Allies and the Empire as well, there was not some policy as to the distribution of the manufacture of the various parts of a shell. He charges that the Shell Committee,
-failing- to endeavour to provide for their construction in Canada, as they might have done, proceeded to give . and award through J. Wesley Allison, in the United States, contracts for fuses amounting to $22,000,000 on which they made an advance of $3,750,000.
That is the charge that is made. Call it whatever you like: call it a charge, or mere fault-finding, as the hon. member for Carle-ton denominated part of his own address, it involves nothing in the way of the honour of a member of the Shell Committee, let alone a member of the Government.
Then he goes on, and here is where what I might call the Pugsleyism of the hon. member for St. John comes in:
That the making of the said contracts through said Allison was unwise and improvident, and was entered into with the knowledge and connivance of the Minister of Militia, and the said Shell Committee failed to obtain delivery of said fuses for an unreasonable time. [DOT]
