Here is another example, according to my hon. friend, of the political end of the business of the Shell Committee. The International Supply Company did get their order for
10,000	shells, but it was on the 12th day of January, 1916, from the Munitions Board, and not from the Shell 'Committee at all. The 'Shell Committee had nothing to do
with it. One of these companies-I will not say which, -because 1 would not like to be wrong-has had its order cancelled since by the Munitions Board for failure to deal fairly with its employees.
Then we come to the third one. We have passed the other two, -and I am sure the hon. 'member is proud of the charges he is levelling against these Ebusiness concerns in Canada and against the Shell Committee, that had nothing to do with them. The Manitoba Bridge and Iron Works are next. The hon- gentleman says that they got an order for 20,000 shells and that not a shell has -been delivered. He had hardly taken his seat until the answer to this libel was hurled at his head in a telegram from the Manitoba Bridge and Iron Works themselves and he was compelled to admit on the floor of Parliament next day that so far from having stated the truth, the actual truth was that that company had had three orders, that the first two they had delivered in full and on 'time, that the third was only given recently and that it would be delivered on time as well. That company has already delivered 47,880 shells, and that is the company which, he says, has not delivered any. Its last order for 20,000 shells was given on the 28th January, 1916, and therefore he brings home guilt to the Shell Committee which went out of office on the 30th November, in the year before," because in giving this contract to the Manitoba Bridge and Iron Works, they were distributing political patronage. The hon. gentleman made a statement in the House -he had. often made it before-as to what he was ready to do and to be interesting I am going to read that statement. He was going to apologise. Here is what he said:
It is true that sometimes we have a lot of difficulty in getting- information and possibly we might not be right exactly to a cent, but I am sufficiently assured of the facts that I am going to read to the House to stake my reputation as a member of that-
I congratulate the hon. gentleman that he did not make the stake any higher.
-if you will give me a committee I will prove them to the hilt or apologize to this House and to the committee and say that I did not know what I am talking about.
In fulfilment ol that contract, it is the duty of the hon. gentleman, in respect to these three companies to which I have already alluded, to admit that he did not kn-ow what he was talking -about and to apologize to the House and to the country. I wait with considerable interest, but with

more interest than hope, to see whether he does so. Well, I pass on to the other seven.
Get up; get up.
Order.
Give us the committee and we will show you.

Now he wants a committee so that he will have a chance to apologise. Having got through with the Manitoba Bridge and Iron Works, I come to the Manitoba Shell Company of St. Boniface. He says they got an order for
10.000	shells, and that none of them have been delivered. They got an order for
10.000	shells, and when did they receive it? -in December, 1915, almost a month after the Shell Committee went out of existence. That is the position of that company, and of course this is another nail in the coffin of the Shell Committee, and a bringing home of the charge that they used their position to distribute political patronage. Now I come to No. 5. The Transcona Shell Company of Winnipeg, he says, got an order for 250,000 shells and nothing delivered. The Transicona Shell Company did get orders for 250,000 shells, hut, so far from having delivered nothing, they have delivered 28,530 shells, and the order fox
200.000	shells was not received until the 4th January, 1916. Perhaps there should be an investigation, but it is not into the Shell Committee. The hon. member for Carleton possibly knows where the investigation is most required. Then, the Vulcan Iron Works are the next offenders. The Vulcan Iron Works Company is a firm, I do not know how large, but of long standing in this country, doing business in Winnipeg when I went there in 1898, and I believe for many years before. That is the next company that comes in for castigation and lampooning at the hands of the hon. member for Carleton.' They got an order for
20.000	shells, and nothing delivered. Well, they got orders for 50,425 shells, and they have already delivered 46,416, and the
20.000	order was not given until the 4th January, 1916. Another apology from the hon. gentleman !
These facts were just as accessible to him as to me. He could get them to-day or to-morrow or any other day, and he has been told that by members of the Government repeatedly. The members of the Munition Board are ready to give any member of Parliament these facts. They do not feel justified in exposing to the country prices

and other matters connected with the resources of the country, but they are ready in regard to these matters to take any member of Parliament into their confidence and reveal to him any facts to which he feels that as a member he has a right.

I wish to state to the
hon. gentleman that within a month I received from the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) a copy of a letter purporting to be from the Chairman of the Munitions Board-I do not have it with me-practically refusing me all the information which my hon. friend is now speaking about .
I do not fully know the contents, of that letter. I am disposed to think-I may be wrong-that the letter stated that if the hon. member would go to the committee he would get the facts.
I will go to the committee.

But they do object to
stating it in writing. At all events, the hon. gentleman can go and get such facts as he desires. He has just as much right to those facts as any other hon. member of this House and will have just as little difficulty in getting them. The Western Shell Committee, he says, got an order for 300,000 shells and not a shell delivered. The fact is that the Western Shell Committee has delivered 198,178 shells. I am of opinion that this Western Shell Committee is a committee of the different factories out there who are doing the work, and while I do not wish to say positively, I have been inclined to believe that this represents other orders, and [DOT]that to count these with the others would mean to count the others twice. However, of [DOT]the orders for 300,000 shells, 198,178 have been delivered.
That concludes the hon. gentleman's allegations as regards the three Prairie Provinces. The bon. member for Carleton, of *course would not give any contracts to those provinces at all. He would *confine his operations to the big trust? in the East. He would ignore the smaller factories everywhere. That is the inevitable conclusion from his argument. He said so in so many words: "Here is the way they have done; here is the way they have lived up to their contract!"-and on the strength of that he libels them before the people of this country and before tin? world. The Vancouver Engineering Works, he says, got an order for 340,000 shells, of which they have

delivered 39,000. They got orders for 30,000, for 15,000 back in the summer, and for 40,000 in October, 1915. Instead of their only having delivered 39,000, they have delivered 66,442, and finally the last two contracts were only made, one on October 8 and one on October 18. These contracts were made under the eye of the British representative, Mr. Thomas, made while he was here, and in fact directing the work of the Shell Committee. Was Mr. Thomas a party to the distribution of political patronage? Over and over again the hon. member for Carleton says in his address:	"Is it
any wonder that the British Government sent out a representative to investigate those things?" It seems never to have occurred to his mind that the very things of which he was complaining were done after the British iGovernment had sent out their representative.
Victoria Machinery Depot of Victoria. I
think this is in the same position as the Western Shell Committee, that is to say, an organization representing those that supply shells. They got an order, he says, for 220,000 and only about 10,000 have been delivered. There have been 12,684 delivered, but the point of the thing is this, that the order for
200.000	shells was obtained on the 18th day of October, 1915, just a little while before the Shell Committee went out of existence, while the British representative himself was here and while every contract was made under his very eye and with his approval.
The Vulcan Iron Works of New Westminster is the last of the ten. He complains because they got orders for 150,000 and only about 35,000 have been delivered. He is wrong as to that, because they have not delivered that many, but it would, of course, be inconsistent on the part of the hon. gentleman to be right, even were the correct figures in his favour. He seems to have made up his mind to have the facts all wrong on one side or on the other. I do not know whether that company has delivered any-my note is not complete in that regard-but they obtained an order for
150.000	on the 19th day of October, 1915; that is to say, they too obtained their order while the Shell Committee had the British representative amongst them, and while he himself was supervising and approved all the work and all the orders.

Will my hon. friend
state now the number of the deliveries that have been made up to a month from the time that I was speaking? because, if he will refer to page 1628 of Hansard, the first
reference I made to those ten companies was as follows:
I find that the Dominion Harvester Company,
of Medicine Hat, were able to get an order for 10,000, and up to a month ago they had not delivered a single shell.

That is exactly what I read, as said by the hon. member for Carleton in respect of the Dominion Harvester Company, but he did not say that in respect of a single other company. But here is the point of the whole affair: the Dominion Harvester Company got its order on the 12th of January, 1916. In the name of common sense how much would my hon. friend expect them to have delivered a month ago?
Will my hon. friend give the information as to what deliveries had been made up to a month ago?

In almost all the cases the orders were given only a few weeks before a month ago. My hon, friend does not, except in respect of that one company, use the words "up to a month ago" when he says that they had not delivered any shells. Why does he seek to modify his language now? but, modify it now as he will, it does not substantiate to the millionth part of a minute any single charge he has made. If they had not made any deliveries up to that time, is that a charge against the Shell Committee, which did not distribute 75 per cent of the orders of which he complained, and which, in regard to the other 25 per cent, distributed them under the eye and under the supervision and approval of Mt. Thomas himself? I was going to say that is a narrow hole to try to get out of, but it is not a hole at all; it is closed absolutely. If the hon. gentleman wants to comply with his contract, he has nothing left to him to do but to apologize to the House at the first opportunity. Why, he says, nothing delivered up to a month ago! The Dominion Harvester Company got a contract on the 12th day of January, 1916-it is an awful thing that they had not delivered anything up to a month ago ! "The Canada Cement Company," he says, "is the company that you should have dealt with and that could have delivered shells." Is my hon. friend aware that the Canada Cement Company took a contract on the 2nd day of November, 1915, and, in respect of part of the contract has not even the plant in yet and has not delivered a shell in respect of any part of the contract?

Does my hon. friend want an answer to that question, because he put his remark in the form of a question? I

am aware that the Canada Cement Company did not agree to furnish the forgings for the first part of their contract; they did agree to furnish the forgings for the second part.
That is right.

They are and have been for some three weeks ready to go on machining shells, but the parties who are responsible for producing the forgings have not done so, and, that is the reason why the Canada Cement Company has not furnished shells.

All the same, why does the hon. gentleman not tell the whole of the truth while he is at it? The Canada Cement Company, when they put in their tender for those shells in relation to which they did not have to supply the forgings, stated that they expected to have the plant ready by the 15th of January, or two and a half months after the contract was let, and, as a matter of fact, they got it ready to commence work in February; that is to say, it took them-I am not making any complaint against them because it is a large plant and would necessarily take a long time to make ready-three months to get ready one plant in relation to one part cf the contract, and in relation to the other part they have not the plant ready yet. Nevertheless, my hon. friend complains that the Dominion Harvester Company had not delivered a month ago shells for which they got the contract on the 12th of January of this year, and he holds up the Canada Cement Company as the company that we ought to have dealt with, and that would have saved the lives of the soldiers at the front.
They are making 9-2 shells, while the others are only making 18-prs.	[DOT]

No, they are not making any at all; they will be making 3.2's later, and doubtless their plant is heavier than that of the other companies. I have not the slightest doubt that the Canada Cement Company are putting the plant down as fast as possible; I believe they have a careful manager; and, further than that, I know it is a fact that, in relation to this order, the Shell Committee were not in a position to let it until very shortly before they did, and, in relation to the other, the correspondence will show that no complaint was made by them against the company at all, but complaint
rMr. Car-veil.]
was made because they were not in a position to get orders of the size and extending over the period for which the Canada Cement Company wanted orders in order to deliver the shells at the price quoted. Any one who has the slightest conception of business knows that a large concern, provided that they can get a large contract extending over a long period' of time, can undertake to deliver at a much cheaper rate than can a smaller concern which has not so large a contract; and a small concern, if it could be arranged with them that they would have all they could make within a year or two years, could make the prices considerably lower than they could in the absence of such an agreement. But the Shell Committee were not in a position to deal without reference to the British Government. They did deal after reference to the British Government, and they gave their contracts under their direction and every price in every instance was approved before a contract was let. Yet we are asked by the hon. member for Carle-ton and the hon. member for St. John to sit in arrogant judgment over the work of the British Government and to tell.them that they know nothing about the price they ought to pay for shells.
I had no thought of detaining the House to so late an hour. I think I have pursued the assertions made by the hon. member for Carleton from end to end of his remarks. I do not know' of anything that I have omitted.	.

You have not referred
to prices yet.
I think I have referred to prices, have I not?
I have not heard it.

I think so, but I did
set out to say this, that I was not going to add to the injury that the hon. member had done to this country by exposing to the people of the world what the British Government do not want revealed. I am going to keep my contract whether the hon. gentleman keeps his or not. I do not pro-PQse to share with him the guilt that he already has brought upon his own head.
The hon. gentleman is not likely to talk prices.
Go on now.

I have said where I will go and where I will stop, and the hon. gentleman shall not persuade me to go further. What does the .hon. gentleman *care? He is ready to sit in judgment on the British Government or any other authority so long as he can bring a little of this counterfeit glory around his own head, and rail and rage and rant before the House -of Commons or make a pyrotechnic display before a committee of the House. These hon. :gentlemen do not want a commission. The hon. member for Carleton is on record more than once as saying they do not want a judge looking into this thing, but what they want is a committee. Why do they not want a commission? I will tell you- it is because they do not want a verdict. All these hon. gentlemen want is a chance to do what they are doing and have been *doing for the last month, under cover of a supposed truce-they want to take stray portions of the evidence, leaving out the contradictions, qualifications, modifying explanations, to take stray portions of the evidence, though these may have been *demonstrated to be false, and scatter broadcast throughout the provinces this poisonous political garbage. That is the policy of these hon. gentlemen.

With the permission of the hon. gentleman I would ask one question before he leaves the point about these western companies. I would like him to look over his notes and see if it is not a fact that the Dominion Harvester Company, of Medicine Hat, received an order for 20,000 shells early in 1915 of which they had not delivered a shell when they got their second order in 1916.

I presume that somebody has sent that to the hon. member. It is not in my notes; there is a note that the Dominion Harvester Company delivered some through the Alberta Foundry and Machine Company as sub-contractors. I do not know whether or not that is what he refers to. At all events, the order of which he complains was given at that later time.
The hon. gentleman is very anxious about the matter of prices. I know enough about that matter to know that for the House of Commons to pass the resolution he supports would be as manifest and blazing folly, having regard to the interest not only of Canada but of this Empire, as was ever perpetrated in a deliberative assembly. I know that whatever prices were made were made by the British Government, without dictation, without suggestion, without supervision, and, consequently, without responsibility, on the part of this Government. I know that the responsible Government for the prices is the Government of Great Britain; and if it is felt by the British people or the British Government that errors were made, and if they will either make an investigation themselves or ask us to make it, we will hasten to comply with their request in whatever form it takes. And no one would be more pleased than myself to receive that request. For, one thing it will do is to remove imputations from the heads of men in this country who have no right to bear those imputations at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite; and another thing it will do is to bring home to the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member of St. John the fact that they stand, and have stood since they made these charges, as *profligate and abandoned slanderers.
Order.
Order.
Let him go on, Mr. Speaker; it does not hurt- anybody.
I would remind the hon. member (Mr. Meighen) that -such language is offensive and unparliamentary.

be conveyed, and I know that if I did that I should be guilty of an offence of which I should not like to be guilty. I have Eound the leader of the Opposition a very fair debater. I did not intend to convey a wrong impression of what he said, and I did not do so. I did leave out something at the beginning and something at the end. I do not know of any way of making an extract except by leaving out something at the beginning and at the end. But I did not leave out anything which modified the view expressed by him in what I quoted. The view he expressed was that, in regard to the motion for the production of papers bearing on transactions made by departments of his Government with the British Government, he would not be justified in granting it, nor would he be justified in referring it to a special committee. He said he would not refer it even to the Public Accounts Committee. He went on to say that if charges were made against the Government, then he would give an investigation. The charges he referred to were charges involving the honor of a minister of the Crown. If such charges had been made here, then it would have been my bounden duty to quote that portion of his speech, because it would have modified the view he expressed in relation to the point I was arguing. But no such charges were made then, as no charges are made now, against the Government, of the nature he meant- and he will not deny he meant charges of that nature, for if he does I can show that that is what he must have meant. Consequently, the remarks I left out had no relation to the point discussed either then or now. He refused in that case even to produce the papers, because he said they related to the conduct of a department of his Government acting for the British Government. I stated that he could not consistently refuse that then, and now say that we should grant an investigation in regard to the conduct of a committee, not a department of the Government at all, nor could he argue, even if they were a department of the Government, that we should grant an investigation. For, even had they been a department of the Government, we would have been in exactly the same position as he was in at that time. I think he was wrong at that time, and that the present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) was right. The war, being over, and the work having been done by a department of the Government, he should have brought down papers. But he refused to do so. I did not then try, and I do not try 
now, to shelter myself or the Government behind the precedent he then established. I think that precedent was wrong. I say that he certainly could not consistently take that position then, and take his present position now. In quoting what I did I quoted everything that bore in the slightest degree upon the argument that I had or upon the argument that was sought to be made by the hon. gentleman himself. I quoted everything that bore in the slightest degree upon the point that was under discussion; the rest bore on another point altogether, upon a subject which did not enter into consideration of the facts at that time and does not enter into consideration of the facts now. I make these remarks only because the leader of the Opposition went pretty far when he said that I had garbled what he said. He did not, however, go so far as certain newspapers have since gone in endeavouring to interpret his remarks. I do not want to be guilty in this House of garbling the remarks of any hon. gentleman; if I cannot argue fairly, I prefer not to argue at all. I may have spoken very strongly with regard to the conduct of the hon. member for Oarleton and of the hon. member for St. John, but they have repeatedly in this House of Commons made assertions in regard to the truth of which they had made no adequate investigation. On the basis of assertions of this kind they have hurled recklessly at the head of various citizens in this country and at the heads of members of the Government-which is not so important a matter- charges of the most reckless and most damaging kind. I do not Relieve that such practice comports with the dignity of Parliament, and I propose whenever it is done to use language as strong as I can, within the rules of Parliament, to rebuke it. I have no personal animosity against these hon. gentlemen; I do believe that I have done no more than my duty as a member of this House in describing, in the only fit language that can be used, the conduct of which they have been guilty in regard to the motion that is before the Chair.
